searchDocs.content: Set the directory where recorded MP4 files will be saved.  bool api_dctvrecord_set_location(GstElement *element, const char *location);   Parameters:  element - dctvrecord GstElementlocation - Directory path for saving MP4 files  Returns:  true on successfalse on failure  info Filenames are automatically generated with timestamps in the format: prefix_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_MSS.mp4 in the respective date directory under location  Example:  api_dctvrecord_set_location(vrecord, "/home/user/recordings");   recordings/ # Directory specified in the location property └── YYYY_MM_DD/ # Date-wise subfolder └── prefix_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_MSS.mp4

In AUTO mode, recording is controlled automatically by MQTT messages.  Example:  // Ensure manual mode is set api_dctvrecord_set_mode(vrecord, DCTVRECORD_MODE_MANUAL); // Start recording api_dctvrecord_set_recording(vrecord, true); // Stop recording api_dctvrecord_set_recording(vrecord, false);

searchDocs.title: Usage Example​
searchDocs.content:
Here's a complete example demonstrating the API usage:  #include "apidctvrecord.h" int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { GstElement *pipeline, *vrecord; // Initialize GStreamer gst_init(&argc, &argv); // Create pipeline pipeline = gst_parse_launch( "videotestsrc ! " "video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480,framerate=30/1 ! " "x264enc tune=zerolatency bitrate=2000 ! " "h264parse config-interval=-1 ! " "video/x-h264,stream-format=avc,alignment=au ! " "dctvrecord name=myrecorder ! " "fakesink", NULL); if (!pipeline) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to create pipeline
"); return -1; } // Get vrecord element vrecord = api_dctvrecord_init(pipeline, "myrecorder"); if (!vrecord) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize vrecord element
"); return -1; } // Configure for automatic recording api_dctvrecord_set_mode(vrecord, DCTVRECORD_MODE_AUTO); api_dctvrecord_set_location(vrecord, "/tmp/recordings"); api_dctvrecord_set_prefix(vrecord, "test"); api_dctvrecord_set_host(vrecord, "192.168.1.100"); api_dctvrecord_set_port(vrecord, 1883); api_dctvrecord_set_mqtt_topic(vrecord, "detections/camera1"); api_dctvrecord_set_det_timeout(vrecord, 10.0); api_dctvrecord_set_auto_enable(vrecord, true); // Start pipeline gst_element_set_state(pipeline, GST_STATE_PLAYING); // Recording starts automatically when detection messages are received printf("Waiting for MQTT detection messages...
"); // Run for 60 seconds sleep(60); // Disable auto recording printf("Disabling auto recording...
"); api_dctvrecord_set_auto_enable(vrecord, false); // Cleanup gst_element_set_state(pipeline, GST_STATE_NULL); api_dctvrecord_deinit(vrecord); gst_object_unref(pipeline); return 0; }

searchDocs.content: mqtt-host​  Specifies the MQTT broker hostname or IP address. searchDocs.title: Bounding Box Styling Properties​
searchDocs.content: bbox-colour​  Specifies the bounding box color as a hex string. Automatically parses to RGB components and optional alpha.  Type: StringDefault: NULL (must use bbox-colour-r/g/b or set via hex)Format: "#RGB", "#RGBA", "#RRGGBB", or "#RRGGBBAA"Access: Read/Write  Alpha in Hex You can specify transparency directly in the hex string using the #RRGGBBAA format. For example, #00FF0080 creates a 50% transparent green (0x80 = 128 = 50% of 255).  Usage:  BashGST API # Green boxes (fully opaque) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour="#00FF00" ... # Red boxes (short format) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour="#F00" ... # Semi-transparent blue boxes (80% opacity) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour="#0000FFCC" ... # Short format with alpha (50% red) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour="#F008" ...     bbox-colour-r, bbox-colour-g, bbox-colour-b​  Specifies the bounding box color in RGB components.  Type: Integer (each component)Default: R=-1, G=-1, B=-1 (not set, must use bbox-colour hex string)Range: -1 (not set) or 0-255Access: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Green boxes gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour-r=0 bbox-colour-g=255 bbox-colour-b=0 ... # Yellow boxes gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-colour-r=255 bbox-colour-g=255 bbox-colour-b=0 ...     bbox-thickness​  Specifies the bounding box border thickness.  Type: IntegerDefault: 2Range: 1-50 pixelsAccess: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay bbox-thickness=2 ...

searchDocs.content: font-type​  Specifies the OpenCV font type for label text.  Type: IntegerDefault: 0 (SIMPLEX)Range: 0-7Access: Read/WriteValues: 0: SIMPLEX1: PLAIN2: DUPLEX3: COMPLEX4: TRIPLEX5: COMPLEX_SMALL6: SCRIPT_SIMPLEX7: SCRIPT_COMPLEX  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay font-type=0 ...     font-scale​  Specifies the font size scale factor.  Type: DoubleDefault: 0.6Range: 0.1-10.0Access: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay font-scale=0.6 ...     label-colour​  Specifies the label text color as a hex string with optional alpha.  Type: StringDefault: NULL (defaults to yellow: #FFFF00)Format: "#RGB", "#RGBA", "#RRGGBB", or "#RRGGBBAA"Access: Read/Write  Usage:  BashGST API # Yellow text (fully opaque) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-colour="#FFFF00" ... # White text gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-colour="#FFF" ... # Semi-transparent white text (80% opacity) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-colour="#FFFFFFCC" ...     font-thickness​  Specifies the font thickness.  Type: IntegerDefault: 2Range: 1-10 pixelsAccess: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay font-thickness=2 ...

searchDocs.title: Label Configuration Properties​
searchDocs.content: draw-label-background​  Enables or disables the label background.  Type: BooleanDefault: trueAccess: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay draw-label-background=true ...     label-bg-colour​  Specifies the label background color as a hex string with optional alpha. When alpha is specified in the hex string, it overrides the label-bg-alpha property.  Type: StringDefault: NULL (uses label-bg-colour-r/g/b values)Format: "#RGB", "#RGBA", "#RRGGBB", or "#RRGGBBAA"Access: Read/Write  Combined Color and Alpha Instead of setting label-bg-colour and label-bg-alpha separately, you can use #RRGGBBAA format to set both at once. For example, #000000B3 creates a 70% opaque black background.  Usage:  BashGST API # Black background (use label-bg-alpha for transparency) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-bg-colour="#000000" label-bg-alpha=0.7 ... # Black background with 70% opacity (alpha in hex) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-bg-colour="#000000B3" ... # Semi-transparent dark blue background (50% opacity) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-bg-colour="#00008080" ...     label-bg-colour-r, label-bg-colour-g, label-bg-colour-b​  Specifies the label background color in RGB components.  Type: Integer (each component)Default: R=0, G=0, B=0 (Black)Range: 0-255Access: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Black background gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-bg-colour-r=0 label-bg-colour-g=0 label-bg-colour-b=0 ...     label-bg-alpha​  Specifies the label background transparency.  Type: DoubleDefault: 0.7Range: 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (opaque)Access: Read/Write  note This property is overridden when alpha is specified in the label-bg-colour hex string (e.g., #000000B3).  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-bg-alpha=0.7 ...     label-position​  Specifies the label position relative to the bounding box.The detection label has boundary detection with a 30-pixel buffer zone that checks if the bounding box is near any screen edge. When a detection approaches the edges, the label automatically repositions itself: moving below the box when near the top edge, adjusting horizontally for left/right edges, or moving inside the box when there's no room outside. Labels now remain fully visible at all times preventing text cutoff regardless of where the tracked object moves on screen.  Type: IntegerDefault: 0 (Top-Left)Access: Read/WriteValues: 0: Top-Left1: Top-Right2: Bottom-Left3: Bottom-Right  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctoverlay label-position=0 ...

searchDocs.title: Basic Build (OpenCV Backend)​
searchDocs.content: # Remove any build directory if already present: rm -rf builddir/ # Setup build directory (default: MACH=opencv) meson setup builddir # Compile ninja -C builddir   Once the compilation is done, the following files among others should be generated in the builddir.  builddir/ # Build directory └── libgstdctoverlay.so # GStreamer plugin

searchDocs.title: Build Options​
searchDocs.content: The plugin supports multiple build configuration options:  Machine Layer Selection​  Since this plugin is implemented in a layered architecture, support for additional rendering backends can be added in mach/ layer of the plugin source. To build the plugin for a specific machine, issue the following command:  # Explicitly specify machine layer meson setup builddir -DMACH=<machine-name>

searchDocs.title: Running the examples​
searchDocs.content: The examples can be run in 2 ways. It can be run in the platform where the plugin and its test code were compiled. Or else, if the compilation was done for a different target platform, then you will have to load the plugins to that target machine.

searchDocs.title: 1. Run the example in the machine where it was compiled​
searchDocs.content: The plugins are output in the builddir directory. So provide the plugin path to Gstreamer before the example pipeline is run.  # Pipeline GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 ...

searchDocs.title: 2. Run the example in a target machine​
searchDocs.content: Upload the plugin to the target platform. Here, we use the adb utility.  # Push the plugin to the plugin directory adb push builddir/libgstdctoverlay.so /usr/lib/gstreamer-1.0/ # Verify installation adb shell gst-inspect-1.0 dctoverlay   note The examples shown here demonstrate usage on both host and target platforms.

searchDocs.title: Basic Detection Overlay​
searchDocs.content: The following example displays detection overlays with default styling.  # Start MQTT broker (in separate terminal) mosquitto -v # Run pipeline with overlay gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay mqtt-host=localhost mqtt-topic=detections ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Captures video from /dev/video8Converts to BGR formatReceives detection data via MQTT from detections topicDraws bounding boxes and labelsDisplays video with overlays

searchDocs.title: Custom Box and Font Styling​
searchDocs.content: The following example uses green boxes with yellow text.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-topic=detections \ box-color-r=0 box-color-g=255 box-color-b=0 \ box-thickness=2 \ font-scale=0.6 \ font-color-r=255 font-color-g=255 font-color-b=0 \ font-thickness=2 ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Green bounding boxes (RGB: 0, 255, 0)Yellow text (RGB: 255, 255, 0)Box thickness: 2 pixelsFont scale: 0.6

searchDocs.title: Label Background Customization​
searchDocs.content: The following example adds semi-transparent black backgrounds to labels.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-topic=detections \ draw-label-background=true \ label-bg-color-r=0 label-bg-color-g=0 label-bg-color-b=0 \ label-bg-alpha=0.7 \ label-position=0 ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Black label background (RGB: 0, 0, 0)70% opacity (alpha: 0.7)Labels positioned at top-left of boxes

searchDocs.title: Confidence Display Configuration​
searchDocs.content: The following example shows confidence scores with 2 decimal places.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-topic=detections \ show-confidence=true \ confidence-decimals=2 ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Displays confidence scores in labelsShows 2 decimal places (e.g., "0.95")

searchDocs.title: ROI Visualization​
searchDocs.content: The following example draws a Region of Interest rectangle.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-topic=detections \ enable-roi=true \ roi-x=100 roi-y=100 roi-width=400 roi-height=300 \ roi-color-r=255 roi-color-g=255 roi-color-b=0 \ roi-thickness=2 ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Draws yellow ROI rectangle (RGB: 255, 255, 0)ROI position: (100, 100) with 400x300 sizeROI thickness: 2 pixels

searchDocs.title: Class Filtering​
searchDocs.content: The following example only displays specific object classes.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-topic=detections \ enable-class-filter=true \ filter-class-ids="0,1,2,5" ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   What it does:  Only draws detections for class IDs 0, 1, 2, and 5Filters out all other classes

searchDocs.title: Complete Configuration Example​
searchDocs.content: The following example demonstrates all customization options.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay \ mqtt-host=localhost \ mqtt-port=1883 \ mqtt-topic=detections \ mqtt-qos=1 \ box-color-r=0 box-color-g=255 box-color-b=0 \ box-thickness=2 \ font-type=0 \ font-scale=0.6 \ font-color-r=255 font-color-g=255 font-color-b=0 \ font-thickness=2 \ draw-label-background=true \ label-bg-color-r=0 label-bg-color-g=0 label-bg-color-b=0 \ label-bg-alpha=0.7 \ label-position=0 \ show-confidence=true \ confidence-decimals=2 \ enable-roi=true \ roi-x=100 roi-y=100 roi-width=400 roi-height=300 \ roi-color-r=255 roi-color-g=255 roi-color-b=0 \ roi-thickness=2 \ enable-class-filter=true \ filter-class-ids="0,1,2" ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink

searchDocs.title: Publishing Detection Data via MQTT​
searchDocs.content: To test the overlay plugin, you need to publish detection data to MQTT. Here's an example Python script:  #!/usr/bin/env python3 import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt import json import time # Create MQTT client client = mqtt.Client() client.connect("localhost", 1883, 60) # Sample detection data detections = { "detections": [ { "bbox": {"x": 100, "y": 50, "width": 200, "height": 150}, "label": "person", "confidence": 0.95, "class_id": 0 }, { "bbox": {"x": 400, "y": 200, "width": 150, "height": 180}, "label": "car", "confidence": 0.87, "class_id": 2 } ] }

searchDocs.title: Debugging​
searchDocs.content: To enable detailed debug output from the plugin, set the GST_DEBUG environment variable before running the pipeline:  export GST_DEBUG=dctoverlay:5   After setting the debug level, run your pipeline to see detailed log messages:  GST_DEBUG=dctoverlay:5 gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,format=BGR ! \ dctoverlay mqtt-host=localhost mqtt-topic=detections ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   Debug levels range from 0 (no output) to 5 (verbose logging). Level 5 provides the most detailed information for troubleshooting.  note If you encounter issues with the plugin: Verify MQTT broker is running: mosquitto -vCheck MQTT connection: mosquitto_sub -h localhost -t detectionsVerify video format is BGR (not RGB)Ensure all dependencies are properly installed

searchDocs.title: Verifying Installation​
searchDocs.content: # Check if plugin is installed gst-inspect-1.0 dctoverlay # Verify properties gst-inspect-1.0 dctoverlay | grep -A 5 "Plugin Details"

searchDocs.title: Basic Build (Without MQTT)​
searchDocs.content: # Remove any build directory if already present: rm -rf builddir/ # Setup build directory (default: MACH_GENERIC, comm=none) meson setup builddir # Compile ninja -C builddir   Once the compilation is done, the following files among other should be generated in the builddir.  builddir/ # Build directory ├── libapidctfcapture.a # Plugin API library ├── libgstdctfcapture.so # GStreamer plugin (plugin interface) ├── test_dctfcapture # Test application for Gstreamer APIs ├── test_api_dctfcapture # Test application for Custom APIs └── selftest # Self test application

searchDocs.title: Build with MQTT Support​
searchDocs.content: To enable MQTT communication framework and AUTO mode functionality:  # Setup build directory with MQTT support meson setup builddir -Dcomm=mqtt # Compile ninja -C builddir   With MQTT enabled, additional files are generated:  builddir/ # Build directory ├── libapidctfcapture.a # Plugin API library ├── libgstdctfcapture.so # GStreamer plugin (with MQTT support) ├── test_dctfcapture # Test application for Gstreamer APIs ├── test_api_dctfcapture # Test application for Custom APIs ├── mqtt_publisher # MQTT publisher test utility ├── test_mqtt_auto_mode # Test application for AUTO mode with MQTT ├── test_mode_change # Test application for runtime mode switching └── selftest # Self test application

searchDocs.title: Build Options​
searchDocs.content: The plugin supports multiple build configuration options:  Machine Layer Selection​  Since this plugin is implemented in a layered architecture, support for additional machines can be added in mach/ layer of the plugin source. To build the plugin and library for a specific machine, issue the following command:  # Explicitly specify machine layer meson setup builddir -Dmach=<machine-name>   Machine Layer Options:  MACH_GENERIC (default): Software implementation using OpenCV  You can find steps to add support for additional machine here.  Communication Framework Selection​  The communication framework determines whether MQTT support is included:  # Build without communication framework (default) meson setup builddir -Dcomm=none # Build with MQTT communication framework meson setup builddir -Dcomm=mqtt   Communication Framework Options:  none (default): No communication framework, MQTT dependencies not requiredmqtt: Enables MQTT communication layer for AUTO mode functionality  Combined Build Options​  You can combine multiple build options:  # Example: Machine-specific build with MQTT support meson setup builddir -Dmach=MACH_GENERIC -Dcomm=mqtt # Example: Reconfigure existing build to enable MQTT meson configure builddir -Dcomm=mqtt ninja -C builddir

searchDocs.title: Running the examples​
searchDocs.content: The examples can be run in 2 ways. It can be run in the platform where the plugin and its test code were compiled. Or else, if the compilation was done for a different target platform, then you will have to load the plugins and the examples to that target machine.

searchDocs.title: 1. Run the example/test in the machine where it was compiled​
searchDocs.content: The plugins and the test code are output in the builddir directory. So provide the plugin path to Gstreamer before the test and the example pipeline are run.  # Pipeline GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 ... # Test app. GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/<test-app>

searchDocs.title: 2. Run the example/test in a target machine​
searchDocs.content: Upload the plugin and test app to the target platform. Here, we use the adb utility.  # Push the plugin to the plugin directory adb push builddir/libgstobd.so <plugin directory> # Eg: /usr/lib/gstreamer-1.0/ # Push the test apps to the execution directory adb push builddir/<test-app> # Enter the adb shell and execute them adb shell shell# ./<test-app>   note The examples shown here are run on the Host PC itself, where the compilation was done.

searchDocs.title: Manual Mode with Prefix​
searchDocs.content: The following example runs in Manual mode and captures 1 frame as the capture flag which is set true captures the first frame and will then be set to false state. Also, the file name will have a prefix appended to it.  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc num-buffers=10 ! \ video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480 ! \ dctfcapture mode=0 location=/tmp prefix=frame capture=true ! \ fakesink   Output: /tmp/frame_2025_10_03_18_03_59_226.jpg

searchDocs.title: Manual Mode without Prefix​
searchDocs.content: The following example runs in Manual mode and captures 1 frame as the capture flag which is set true captures the first frame and will then be set to false state.  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc num-buffers=10 ! \ video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480 ! \ dctfcapture mode=0 location=/tmp capture=true ! \ fakesink   Output: /tmp/2025_10_03_18_04_16_008.jpg

searchDocs.title: Periodic Mode​
searchDocs.content: The following example runs in Periodic mode and captures a frame every 3 seconds as the time-period is set to 3 seconds.  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! \ video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480 ! \ dctfcapture mode=1 time-period=3 location=/tmp prefix=capture ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   Captures every 3 seconds with timestamped filenames:  /tmp/capture_2025_10_03_18_03_59_226.jpg/tmp/capture_2025_10_03_18_04_02_312.jpg/tmp/capture_2025_10_03_18_04_05_401.jpg

searchDocs.title: AUTO Mode (MQTT-based Object Detection)​
searchDocs.content: note AUTO mode requires the plugin to be built with MQTT support: meson setup builddir -Dcomm=mqtt  The following example runs in AUTO mode and captures frames when object detection messages arrive via MQTT:  # Start MQTT broker (in separate terminal) mosquitto -v # Run pipeline with AUTO mode GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! \ video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480 ! \ dctfcapture mode=2 mqtt-topic=object/detection \ mqtt-host=localhost mqtt-port=1883 time-skip=100 \ location=/tmp prefix=detected ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink   note Requires a running MQTT broker (Mosquitto) and a publisher sending object detection messages to the configured topic.  MQTT Message Format (JSON):  { "objects_detected": true, "count": 2, "objects": [ {"class": "person", "confidence": 0.95}, {"class": "car", "confidence": 0.87} ] }   Captures on object detection with timestamped filenames:  /tmp/detected_2025_10_09_14_30_45_123.jpg/tmp/detected_2025_10_09_14_30_45_678.jpg

searchDocs.title: AUTO Mode with Remote Broker​
searchDocs.content: Connect to a remote MQTT broker:  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir gst-launch-1.0 videotestsrc ! \ video/x-raw,format=I420,width=640,height=480 ! \ dctfcapture mode=2 mqtt-topic=camera/detection \ mqtt-host=192.168.1.100 mqtt-port=1883 time-skip=0 \ location=/tmp prefix=remote ! \ videoconvert ! autovideosink

searchDocs.title: 1. Self-Test (Automated Comprehensive Tests)​
searchDocs.content: Automated test suite that validates all plugin functionality:  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/selftest   Test Coverage:  Manual mode capture with prefixManual mode capture without prefixPeriodic mode capture (time-based intervals)API getter functionsRuntime property modification  Exit code 0 indicates all tests passed.

searchDocs.title: 2. GStreamer-based Test (test_dctfcapture)​
searchDocs.content: Interactive test using direct GStreamer API:  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/test_dctfcapture

searchDocs.title: 3. API-based Test (test_api_dctfcapture)​
searchDocs.content: Interactive test using the simplified C API:  GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/test_api_dctfcapture   The interactive tests provide prompts to:  Select capture mode (Manual/Periodic)Set time period (for Periodic mode)Automatically test the selected configuration

searchDocs.title: 4. MQTT AUTO Mode Test (test_mqtt_auto_mode)​
searchDocs.content: note Requires build with MQTT support: meson setup builddir -Dcomm=mqtt  Test AUTO mode with MQTT object detection:  # Start MQTT broker first mosquitto -v # Run AUTO mode test (captures for 10 seconds) GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/test_mqtt_auto_mode 10   What it tests:  MQTT connection to broker (localhost:1883)Subscription to "object/detection" topicFrame capture on object detection messagesThrottling with time-skip configurationAuto-reconnection on broker restart  Usage:  ./builddir/test_mqtt_auto_mode <duration_seconds>

searchDocs.title: 5. Mode Change Test (test_mode_change)​
searchDocs.content: note Requires build with MQTT support: meson setup builddir -Dcomm=mqtt  Test runtime mode switching and MQTT connection management:  # Start MQTT broker first mosquitto -v # Run mode change test GST_PLUGIN_PATH=builddir ./builddir/test_mode_change   What it tests:  MANUAL → AUTO mode switching (MQTT connects)AUTO → PERIODIC mode switching (MQTT disconnects)PERIODIC → AUTO mode switching (MQTT reconnects)Resource cleanup during mode transitionsRuntime property reconfiguration

searchDocs.title: Core Dependencies (Always Required)​
searchDocs.content: GStreamer >= 1.0GStreamer Base >= 1.0GStreamer Video >= 1.0OpenCV 4 (for MACH_GENERIC)Meson >= 0.54  Install on Ubuntu/Debian:  sudo apt-get install libgstreamer1.0-dev libgstreamer-plugins-base1.0-dev \ libopencv-dev meson ninja-build

searchDocs.title: MQTT Communication Dependencies (Optional)​
searchDocs.content: Only required when building with -Dcomm=mqtt option:  Mosquitto MQTT client library (libmosquitto-dev)Mosquitto broker (for testing)  Install on Ubuntu/Debian:  sudo apt-get install libmosquitto-dev mosquitto mosquitto-clients   note MQTT dependencies are only required if you build with -Dcomm=mqtt to enable AUTO mode (mode=2) for event-driven capture. If you don't need MQTT functionality, you can build without these dependencies using the default build configuration.

searchDocs.title: location​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the directory path where the MP4 video files need to be saved. This property is mandatory to be set before running the element in a pipeline.  Type: StringDefault: NULLAccess: Read/Write  If /home/user/videos is the target location , then :  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord location=/home/user/videos ...   warning The user must verify that the location value passed is an actual existing directory. If the directory doesn't exist, then dctvrecord will fail to start the recording operation.

searchDocs.title: prefix​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the prefix that needs to be prepended to the file names.  Type: StringDefault: NULLAccess: Read/Write  If CAM1 is the prefix, then :  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord prefix=CAM1 ...   The files will be saved as follows:  With prefix: <PREFIX>_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_MSS.mp4Without prefix: YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_MSS.mp4

searchDocs.title: recording​
searchDocs.content: In MANUAL mode, writing true to this property will start recording, false will stop recording.  Type: BooleanDefault: falseAccess: Read/Write (MANUAL mode), Read-only (AUTO mode)  note This property is only valid in MANUAL mode. In AUTO mode, recording property has no role in controlling the video recording.  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Start recording (Manual mode) gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=0 recording=true ...

searchDocs.title: mode​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the recording mode. This plugin can record in 2 modes:  Mode	DescriptionManual (0)	User manually controls recording via API Auto (1)	Automatic recording based on MQTT object detection messages  Type: Integer [0/1]Default: 0Access: Read/Write  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Manual mode gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=0 ... # AUTO mode gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 ...

searchDocs.title: auto-enable​
searchDocs.content: Enables or disables the automatic recording feature in Auto mode. When enabled, the plugin connects to MQTT broker and starts monitoring for detection messages.  Type: BooleanDefault: trueAccess: Read/Write  note This property is only effective in Auto mode. Setting this to true initiates MQTT connection. Setting to false disconnects from MQTT and stops recording.  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Enable automatic recording gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 auto-enable=true mqtt-topic=detections/camera1 ...   note Before setting auto-enable property to true, ensure that the properties location, mqtt-topicand mode are set correctly.

searchDocs.title: host​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the MQTT broker host address to connect to in Auto mode.  Type: StringDefault: "localhost"Access: Read/Write  note This property is protocol-agnostic and will be used for future TCP and Kafka support. Currently only MQTT is supported.  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 host=192.168.1.100 port=1883 ...

searchDocs.title: port​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the MQTT broker port to connect to in Auto mode.  Type: IntegerDefault: 1883Range: 1-65535Access: Read/Write  note This property is protocol-agnostic and will be used for future TCP and Kafka support. Currently only MQTT is supported (default port: 1883).  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 host=192.168.1.100 port=1883 ...

searchDocs.title: mqtt-topic​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the MQTT topic to subscribe for object detection messages in Auto mode. When detections are received on this topic, recording automatically starts. If auto-enable is true.  Type: StringDefault: NULLAccess: Read/Write  note This property is only effective in Auto mode. Setting this property when auto-enable is true will automatically connect to the broker.  If camera/detections is the topic name, then :  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 host=192.168.1.100 port=1883 \ auto-enable=true mqtt-topic=camera/detections ...   MQTT Message Format (JSON):  The plugin expects JSON messages with the following structure:  { "timestamp": 1760334623.003448, "detections": [ {"class": "person", "class_index":56, "confidence": 0.95, "bbox":{"x":0.703,"y":0.469,"width":0.292,"height":0.474}}, {"class": "car", "class_index":56, "confidence": 0.95, "bbox":{"x":0.703,"y":0.469,"width":0.292,"height":0.474}} ] }   When detections contain a class, Recording startsWhen detections is empty, waits for det-timeout and then stops recording.If no messages received for det-timeout seconds, recording stops

searchDocs.title: det-timeout​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the timeout period after which the recording is supposed to stop if no detections are present.  Type: Double (Floating point)Default: 10.0Range: > 0.0 secondsAccess: Read/Write  note This property is effective only in Auto mode.  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API # Stop recording after 7 seconds of no detections gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 det-timeout=7.0 ...

searchDocs.title: mqtt-client-id​
searchDocs.content: Specifies the client id with which the element is going to establish connection with the mqtt broker  Type: StringDefault: <element-name>-<pid>Access: Read/Write  note This property is useful only in Auto mode.  Usage:  BashWith APIGST API gst-launch-1.0 ... ! dctvrecord mode=1 mqtt-client-id="newelement" ...   note Apart from the specified properties, this plugin also contains some extra properties that are related to the sink architecture in gstreamer. All of them are not tested.

searchDocs.title: Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before building, ensure you have the following dependencies installed:  Meson build system (>= 0.54)Ninja build toolC++17 compatible compiler (g++ or clang++)libmosquitto (MQTT client library) - required if building with MQTTlibcjson (JSON parsing) - required if building with MQTTPTZ control library - required if building with PTZ support

searchDocs.title: Installing Dependencies​
searchDocs.content: On Debian/Ubuntu systems:  sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install meson ninja-build g++ libmosquitto-dev libcjson-dev   Yocto SDK Toolchain Setup For standalone SDK builds using the Yocto toolchain, you must first create and source the SDK environment before building. See the Toolchain Setup documentation for instructions on creating and installing the SDK toolchain. # Source the SDK environment source /path/to/sdk/environment-setup-<arch>-poky-linux # Then proceed with building cd sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack meson setup build meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: Build Options​
searchDocs.content: The library supports the following build-time configuration options:  Option	Values	Default	Descriptioncomm	mqtt, none	mqtt	Communication framework for receiving detections ptz	enabled, disabled	disabled	PTZ hardware control support

searchDocs.title: 1. Configure Build​
searchDocs.content: cd sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack meson setup build

searchDocs.title: 2. Build Library​
searchDocs.content: meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: 3. Install Library​
searchDocs.content: meson install -C build   This installs:  Shared library: libpid_otrack.so → $PREFIX/lib/Header files: *.h → $PREFIX/include/pid-otrack/

searchDocs.title: Build with MQTT Communication (Default)​
searchDocs.content: meson setup build -Dcomm=mqtt meson compile -C build   This enables:  MQTT client for receiving object detectionsJSON parsing for detection messagesPreprocessor define: -DCOMM_MQTT

searchDocs.title: Build without Communication Layer​
searchDocs.content: meson setup build -Dcomm=none meson compile -C build   This creates a standalone library for manual detection updates.  Preprocessor define: -DDISABLE_MQTT

searchDocs.title: Build with PTZ Control Support​
searchDocs.content: meson setup build -Dcomm=mqtt -Dptz=enabled meson compile -C build   This enables hardware PTZ control integration.  Preprocessor define: -DPTZ_ENABLEDLinks with: libptctrl.a  PTZ TCP Server Required When building with -Dptz=enabled, you must run the PTZ TCP server (test/ptz_tcp_server.py) before running the test application, otherwise it will fail at initialization. See PTZ TCP Server Setup section below for details.

searchDocs.title: Custom Build Configuration​
searchDocs.content: meson setup build \ -Dcomm=mqtt \ -Dptz=enabled \ -Dbuildtype=release \ -Dprefix=/usr/local meson compile -C build meson install -C build

searchDocs.title: Build Types​
searchDocs.content: Configure build type using -Dbuildtype:  Build Type	Optimization	Debug Info	Use Casedebug	-O0	Full	Development debugoptimized	-O2 -g	Yes	Testing (default) release	-O3	Minimal	Production minsize	-Os	No	Embedded systems

searchDocs.title: Reconfigure Build​
searchDocs.content: To change build options after initial setup:  meson configure build -Dcomm=none -Dptz=disabled meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: Clean Build​
searchDocs.content: rm -rf build meson setup build meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: Test Application​
searchDocs.content: The library includes a test application (test_pid_otrack) for validating functionality.

searchDocs.title: Building Test Application​
searchDocs.content: The test application is automatically built with the library:  meson compile -C build   Test executable location: build/test_pid_otrack

searchDocs.title: Running Test Application​
searchDocs.content: ./build/test_pid_otrack   The test application demonstrates:  Library initializationDetection updatesPID control calculationsMode switchingTarget selection

searchDocs.title: PTZ TCP Server Setup​
searchDocs.content: Required for PTZ-Enabled Builds If you built the library with -Dptz=enabled, the test application will fail unless the PTZ TCP server is running.

searchDocs.title: Why is this needed?​
searchDocs.content: The test application initializes PTZ control at startup. If built with PTZ enabled, it calls pt_init() which attempts to connect to the PTZ TCP server. If the server is not running, initialization will fail:  [ERROR] Failed to initialize PTZ control Make sure the PTZ TCP server is running!

searchDocs.title: Starting the PTZ TCP Server​
searchDocs.content: The library includes a Python-based PTZ TCP server simulator for testing purposes.  Location: test/ptz_tcp_server.py  Usage:  # Make the script executable chmod +x sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack/test/ptz_tcp_server.py # Start server on all interfaces (default port 5005) ./sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack/test/ptz_tcp_server.py # Or specify custom host and port ./sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack/test/ptz_tcp_server.py --host 169.254.11.105 --port 5005 # Or start on localhost only ./sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack/test/ptz_tcp_server.py --host 127.0.0.1   Server Options:  --host HOST: Host address to bind to (default: 0.0.0.0 - all interfaces)--port PORT: Port to listen on (default: 5005)-h, --help: Show help message

searchDocs.title: Running Test with PTZ Server​
searchDocs.content: Open two terminal windows:  Terminal 1 - Start PTZ Server:  cd sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack ./test/ptz_tcp_server.py --host 169.254.11.105 --port 5005   Terminal 2 - Run Test Application:  cd build ./test_pid_otrack

searchDocs.title: Alternative: Build Without PTZ​
searchDocs.content: If you don't need PTZ control or don't want to run the TCP server, rebuild without PTZ support:  # Reconfigure existing build meson configure build -Dptz=disabled meson compile -C build # Or clean build rm -rf build meson setup build -Dcomm=mqtt -Dptz=disabled meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: Cross-Compilation​
searchDocs.content: For cross-compilation with Yocto SDK:  source /path/to/yocto/sdk/environment-setup-script meson setup build --cross-file=cross-compile.ini meson compile -C build

searchDocs.title: Build Issues​
searchDocs.content: Error: dependency 'libmosquitto' not found  Install MQTT library: sudo apt-get install libmosquitto-devOr build without MQTT: meson setup build -Dcomm=none  Error: dependency 'libcjson' not found  Install cJSON: sudo apt-get install libcjson-devOr build without MQTT: meson setup build -Dcomm=none  Error: PTZ library not found  Ensure lib/ptz/libptctrl.a existsOr build without PTZ: meson setup build -Dptz=disabled

searchDocs.title: Runtime Issues​
searchDocs.content: Test application fails with "Failed to initialize PTZ control"  Cause: Built with PTZ enabled but PTZ TCP server is not runningSolution 1: Start the PTZ TCP server before running the test (see above)Solution 2: Rebuild without PTZ support

searchDocs.title: Features​
searchDocs.content: PID-based Camera Control: Smooth pan/tilt camera movements using PID control algorithmsMultiple Tracking Modes: Support for centroid tracking and ROI (Region of Interest) trackingMQTT Communication: Real-time object detection data reception via MQTT protocolDynamic Target Selection: Select targets by ID or display coordinatesResolution Independence: Automatic coordinate conversion between model and display resolutionsThread-Safe: Mutex-protected API for multi-threaded applicationsConfigurable Parameters: Adjustable PID gains, filtering, and tracking parametersPTZ Control Support: Optional integration with hardware PTZ controllers (build option)Modular Architecture: Clean separation between library interface, logic, and communication layers

searchDocs.title: Requirements​
searchDocs.content: To use the PID Object Tracker library, you will need the following dependencies:  Build System: Meson (>= 0.54) and NinjaCompiler: C++17 compatible compilerMQTT Support (optional): libmosquitto and libcjsonPTZ Control (optional): PTZ control library

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: cd sentinal_sdk/image/pid_otrack meson setup build meson compile -C build meson install -C build

searchDocs.title: Basic Usage​
searchDocs.content: #include "lib-pid-otrack.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; int main() { // Initialize tracker FrameResolution model_res(640, 384); FrameResolution display_res(1920, 1080); ObjectTrackerLib tracker(model_res, display_res); // Configure tracker tracker.initializeWithConfig("my_app"); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(1); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode::CENTROID); tracker.ai_obj_trk_enable(); // Simulate detection updates std::vector<DetectedObject> detections = { DetectedObject(1, 100, 150, 80, 120, 0.95f) }; tracker.ai_obj_trk_update_detections(detections); // Calculate pan/tilt command PanTiltCommand cmd = tracker.calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { printf("Pan: %.2f, Tilt: %.2f\n", cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Tracking Modes​
searchDocs.content: The library supports two tracking modes:

searchDocs.title: CENTROID Mode​
searchDocs.content: Keeps the tracked object at the frame center. This mode calculates PID commands to move the camera so that the object's center point aligns with the display center.  tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode::CENTROID);

searchDocs.title: ROI Mode​
searchDocs.content: Keeps the tracked object within a defined Region of Interest (ROI). The camera only moves when the object approaches or exits the ROI boundaries.  tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode::ROI); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_roi(400.0f, 200.0f, 1120.0f, 680.0f);

searchDocs.title: Performance Considerations​
searchDocs.content: Thread Safety: All public APIs are mutex-protectedMemory: Minimal allocations in steady-state operationCPU: PID calculations are lightweight (<1% CPU @ 30 Hz)Latency: End-to-end latency ~33ms @ 30 FPS detection rate

searchDocs.title: Toolchain for Sentinel SoM
searchDocs.content: Toolchain for Sentinel SoM This document describes the procurement and usage of toolchain to work with Sentinel SoM. In order to compile and work with user applications, Yocto provides a toolchain that helps the programmer to create a build environment of Sentinel SoM on a host machine. To generate the toolchain of sentinel-media-oobe image for sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1 machine, execute the following commands in the build system : docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):$(pwd) -v ~/.ssh/:/home/pokyuser/.ssh ghcr.io/synaptics-astra/crops:1.0.0 --workdir=$(pwd) OOBE=enabled MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment bitbake sentinel-media-oobe -c populate_sdk note Building with populate_sdk to obtain the toolchain for the first time may take sometime to complete depending on the capabilities of the build system. This will create a script in build/tmp/deploy/sdk/ directory. In this case, the script will be poky-glibc-x86_64-sentinel-media-oobe-cortexa73-sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-toolchain-4.0.17.sh. Copy this script to the system on which you want to run the toolchain and execute the script. A prompt will be shown to select the target directory to which the toolchain needs to be installed. To opt for the default location, press enter without specifying the taget directory. If no issues are present, the toolchain will be successfully installed on the host machine. In order to activate the toolchain, source the environment setup script present in the target directory. In this case, source /opt/poky/4.0.17/environment-setup-cortexa73-poky-linux

searchDocs.title: Configuration APIs​
searchDocs.content: Tracking Enable/Disable​  void ai_obj_trk_enable(); void ai_obj_trk_disable(); bool ai_obj_trk_is_enabled() const;   Enable or disable object tracking. When disabled, calculatePanTiltCommand() returns invalid commands.    Resolution Configuration​  void ai_obj_trk_set_model_resolution(int width, int height); void ai_obj_trk_set_display_resolution(int width, int height); void ai_obj_trk_set_resolutions(int model_width, int model_height, int display_width, int display_height);   Configure the resolution settings. The tracker automatically converts coordinates between model and display space.  Parameters:  width, height: Resolution dimensions in pixelsmodel_width, model_height: Model resolution dimensionsdisplay_width, display_height: Display resolution dimensions    Target Selection​  bool ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(int id); int ai_obj_trk_get_target_id() const; bool ai_obj_trk_set_by_coordinate(float x, float y);   Select which object to track. You can select by tracking ID or by clicking coordinates.  Parameters:  id: Tracking ID of the object to followx, y: Display coordinates (the closest object to these coordinates will be selected)  Returns: true if target was set successfully    Tracking Mode​  bool ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode mode); TrackingMode ai_obj_trk_get_mode() const;   Set the tracking mode: CENTROID (keep object at center) or ROI (keep object within ROI bounds).  Parameters:  mode: Either TrackingMode::CENTROID or TrackingMode::ROI  Returns: true if mode was set successfully    ROI Configuration​  bool ai_obj_trk_set_roi(float x, float y, float width, float height); ROI ai_obj_trk_get_roi() const;   Configure the Region of Interest for ROI tracking mode.  Parameters:  x, y: Top-left corner coordinates (in display space)width, height: ROI dimensions  Returns: true if ROI was set successfully    PID Tuning​  void ai_obj_trk_set_pid_gains(float pan_kp, float pan_ki, float pan_kd, float tilt_kp, float tilt_ki, float tilt_kd); void ai_obj_trk_reset_pid_controllers(); void ai_obj_trk_set_pid_limits(float min_output, float max_output); void ai_obj_trk_set_filtering_params(float deadband_threshold, float smoothing_factor);   Fine-tune PID controller parameters for optimal tracking performance.  Parameters:  pan_kp, tilt_kp: Proportional gains (default: 0.10)pan_ki, tilt_ki: Integral gains (default: 0.001)pan_kd, tilt_kd: Derivative gains (default: 0.015)min_output, max_output: Output limits (default: -60.0, 60.0)deadband_threshold: Minimum error to generate command (default: 0.05)smoothing_factor: Output smoothing factor 0-1 (default: 0.8)

searchDocs.title: DetectedObject​
searchDocs.content: Represents a detected and tracked object.  struct DetectedObject { int id; // Object tracking ID float x, y; // Center coordinates float width, height; // Bounding box dimensions float confidence; // Detection confidence (0.0 to 1.0) };   Fields:  id: Unique tracking ID (persistent across frames)x, y: Object center coordinates in model resolutionwidth, height: Bounding box dimensionsconfidence: Detection confidence score (0.0 = 0%, 1.0 = 100%)

searchDocs.title: FrameResolution​
searchDocs.content: Defines frame dimensions.  struct FrameResolution { int width; // Frame width in pixels int height; // Frame height in pixels };

searchDocs.title: PanTiltCommand​
searchDocs.content: Output structure containing camera movement commands.  struct PanTiltCommand { float pan_delta; // Horizontal movement (-1.0 to 1.0) float tilt_delta; // Vertical movement (-1.0 to 1.0) bool valid; // Whether command is valid };   Fields:  pan_delta: Horizontal camera movement (-1.0 = left, 1.0 = right, 0.0 = no movement)tilt_delta: Vertical camera movement (-1.0 = down, 1.0 = up, 0.0 = no movement)valid: Set to true if command contains valid data (tracking enabled and target found)

searchDocs.title: ROI (Region of Interest)​
searchDocs.content: Defines a rectangular region for ROI tracking mode.  struct ROI { float x, y; // Top-left corner coordinates float width, height; // ROI dimensions std::pair<float, float> getCenter() const; };   Methods:  getCenter(): Returns the center point coordinates of the ROI

searchDocs.title: MQTTConfig​
searchDocs.content: MQTT connection configuration.  struct MQTTConfig { std::string broker_host; // MQTT broker hostname/IP int broker_port; // MQTT broker port (default: 1883) std::string client_id; // MQTT client identifier std::string detection_topic; // Topic for object detections std::string username; // MQTT username (optional) std::string password; // MQTT password (optional) int keepalive; // Keep-alive interval (default: 60) bool clean_session; // Clean session flag (default: true) int qos; // Quality of Service (default: 1) };   Example:  MQTTConfig config; config.broker_host = "192.168.1.100"; config.broker_port = 1883; config.client_id = "camera_tracker"; config.detection_topic = "ai/detections/camera1";

searchDocs.title: TrackerConfig​
searchDocs.content: Advanced tracker configuration parameters.  struct TrackerConfig { // PID output limits float pid_output_min; // Default: -60.0 float pid_output_max; // Default: 60.0 // Command filtering float deadband_threshold; // Default: 0.05 float smoothing_factor; // Default: 0.8 // Time delta limits float min_time_delta; // Default: 0.001 (1ms) float max_time_delta; // Default: 1.0 (1s) float default_time_delta; // Default: 0.033 (~30 FPS) // Resolution limits int max_resolution_dimension; // Default: 10000 // ROI defaults float default_roi_width_percent; // Default: 0.2 (20%) float default_roi_height_percent; // Default: 0.28 (28%) // PID gain limits float max_proportional_gain; // Default: 10.0 float max_integral_gain; // Default: 1.0 };

searchDocs.title: TrackingMode​
searchDocs.content: enum class TrackingMode { CENTROID, // Keep object at frame center ROI // Keep object within defined ROI };   Values:  CENTROID: Camera adjusts to keep the tracked object at the center of the frameROI: Camera only moves when the object approaches or exits the ROI boundaries

searchDocs.title: LogLevel​
searchDocs.content: enum class LogLevel { LOG_DEBUG = 0, INFO = 1, WARNING = 2, ERROR = 3, NONE = 4 };   Example:  ObjectTrackerLib::setLogLevel(LogLevel::LOG_DEBUG);

searchDocs.title: MQTT Message Format​
searchDocs.content: The library expects object detection messages in JSON format:  { "detections": [ { "id": 1, "x": 320, "y": 240, "width": 80, "height": 120, "confidence": 0.95, "class": "person" } ] }   Field Descriptions:  id: Tracking ID (persistent across frames)x, y: Center coordinates in model resolutionwidth, height: Bounding box dimensionsconfidence: Detection confidence score (0.0 to 1.0)class: Object class name (optional, not used by tracker)

searchDocs.title: Example 1: Basic Tracking (Manual Updates)​
searchDocs.content: This example shows basic object tracking with manual detection updates, suitable for integration with custom detection pipelines.  #include "lib-pid-otrack.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; int main() { // Initialize tracker with model and display resolutions FrameResolution model_res(640, 384); FrameResolution display_res(1920, 1080); ObjectTrackerLib tracker(model_res, display_res); // Configure tracker tracker.initializeWithConfig("my_app"); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(1); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode::CENTROID); tracker.ai_obj_trk_enable(); // Main tracking loop while (running) { // Get detections from your detection pipeline std::vector<DetectedObject> detections = getDetectionsFromPipeline(); // Update tracker with new detections tracker.ai_obj_trk_update_detections(detections); // Calculate pan/tilt command PanTiltCommand cmd = tracker.calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { printf("Pan: %.2f, Tilt: %.2f\n", cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); // Send commands to PTZ controller sendToPTZController(cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } usleep(33000); // ~30 Hz control rate } return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Example 2: MQTT-Based Tracking​
searchDocs.content: This example demonstrates automatic tracking with MQTT-based detection updates, ideal for distributed systems.  #include "mqtt-object-tracker.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; int main() { // Initialize MQTT tracker FrameResolution model_res(640, 384); FrameResolution display_res(1920, 1080); MQTTObjectTracker mqtt_tracker(model_res, display_res); // Configure MQTT connection MQTTConfig mqtt_config; mqtt_config.broker_host = "192.168.1.100"; mqtt_config.broker_port = 1883; mqtt_config.client_id = "camera_tracker"; mqtt_config.detection_topic = "ai/detections/camera1"; mqtt_config.username = ""; // Optional mqtt_config.password = ""; // Optional if (!mqtt_tracker.initializeMQTT(mqtt_config)) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize MQTT\n"); return -1; } if (!mqtt_tracker.startMQTT()) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to start MQTT\n"); return -1; } // Configure tracking parameters auto* tracker = mqtt_tracker.getTracker(); tracker->initializeWithConfig("mqtt_app"); tracker->ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(1); tracker->ai_obj_trk_enable(); // Main tracking loop // Detections are automatically received via MQTT while (running) { if (tracker->ai_obj_trk_is_enabled()) { PanTiltCommand cmd = tracker->calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { // Control camera based on cmd.pan_delta and cmd.tilt_delta control_camera(cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } } usleep(100000); // 10 Hz control rate } // Cleanup mqtt_tracker.stopMQTT(); return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Example 3: ROI-Based Tracking​
searchDocs.content: This example shows how to use Region of Interest (ROI) tracking mode, where the camera only moves when the object approaches ROI boundaries.  #include "lib-pid-otrack.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; int main() { // Initialize tracker ObjectTrackerLib tracker( FrameResolution(640, 384), FrameResolution(1920, 1080) ); tracker.initializeWithConfig("roi_app"); // Configure ROI mode with custom ROI tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_mode(TrackingMode::ROI); // Define ROI as center 60% of frame float roi_x = 1920 * 0.2; // 20% from left float roi_y = 1080 * 0.2; // 20% from top float roi_width = 1920 * 0.6; // 60% of width float roi_height = 1080 * 0.6; // 60% of height tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_roi(roi_x, roi_y, roi_width, roi_height); // Select target and enable tracking tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(1); tracker.ai_obj_trk_enable(); // Main tracking loop while (running) { std::vector<DetectedObject> detections = getDetections(); tracker.ai_obj_trk_update_detections(detections); PanTiltCommand cmd = tracker.calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { // Camera only moves when object approaches ROI edges controlPTZ(cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } usleep(33000); } return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Example 4: PID Tuning for Different Scenarios​
searchDocs.content: This example demonstrates how to tune PID parameters for different tracking scenarios.  #include "lib-pid-otrack.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; // Aggressive tracking (fast response, may be jittery) void configureAggressiveTracking(ObjectTrackerLib& tracker) { tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_gains( 0.20f, // pan_kp - higher for faster response 0.002f, // pan_ki 0.020f, // pan_kd 0.20f, // tilt_kp 0.002f, // tilt_ki 0.020f // tilt_kd ); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_limits(-80.0f, 80.0f); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_filtering_params(0.02f, 0.6f); // Less smoothing } // Smooth tracking (slower response, more stable) void configureSmoothTracking(ObjectTrackerLib& tracker) { tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_gains( 0.08f, // pan_kp - lower for gentler response 0.001f, // pan_ki 0.012f, // pan_kd - higher to reduce overshoot 0.08f, // tilt_kp 0.001f, // tilt_ki 0.012f // tilt_kd ); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_limits(-50.0f, 50.0f); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_filtering_params(0.05f, 0.9f); // More smoothing } // Balanced tracking (default settings) void configureBalancedTracking(ObjectTrackerLib& tracker) { tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_gains( 0.10f, // pan_kp 0.001f, // pan_ki 0.015f, // pan_kd 0.10f, // tilt_kp 0.001f, // tilt_ki 0.015f // tilt_kd ); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_pid_limits(-60.0f, 60.0f); tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_filtering_params(0.03f, 0.8f); } int main() { ObjectTrackerLib tracker( FrameResolution(640, 384), FrameResolution(1920, 1080) ); tracker.initializeWithConfig("tuning_app"); // Choose tracking style based on your needs configureSmoothTracking(tracker); // For surveillance cameras // configureAggressiveTracking(tracker); // For sports tracking // configureBalancedTracking(tracker); // For general use tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_target_id(1); tracker.ai_obj_trk_enable(); // Tracking loop... return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Example 5: Dynamic Topic Switching​
searchDocs.content:
This example shows how to dynamically switch between different MQTT topics at runtime, useful for multi-camera systems.  #include "mqtt-object-tracker.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; void switchToCamera(MQTTObjectTracker& tracker, const std::string& old_topic, const std::string& new_topic) { // Unsubscribe from old camera topic if (!old_topic.empty()) { tracker.unsubscribe(old_topic); printf("Unsubscribed from: %s
", old_topic.c_str()); } // Subscribe to new camera topic if (tracker.subscribe(new_topic, 1)) { tracker.setDetectionTopic(new_topic); printf("Switched to: %s
", new_topic.c_str()); } else { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to subscribe to: %s
", new_topic.c_str()); } } int main() { MQTTObjectTracker tracker( FrameResolution(640, 384), FrameResolution(1920, 1080) ); // Initialize MQTT MQTTConfig config; config.broker_host = "localhost"; config.broker_port = 1883; config.client_id = "multi_camera_tracker"; config.detection_topic = "camera/cam1/detections"; tracker.initializeMQTT(config); tracker.startMQTT(); auto* obj_tracker = tracker.getTracker(); obj_tracker->initializeWithConfig("multi_cam_app"); obj_tracker->ai_obj_trk_enable(); std::string current_topic = "camera/cam1/detections"; // Main loop while (running) { // Check for camera switch command (e.g., from user input) if (shouldSwitchCamera()) { std::string new_topic = getNewCameraTopic(); switchToCamera(tracker, current_topic, new_topic); current_topic = new_topic; } // Process tracking PanTiltCommand cmd = obj_tracker->calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { controlCamera(cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } usleep(100000); } tracker.stopMQTT(); return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Example 6: Interactive Target Selection​
Example 7: Multi-Resolution Support​
searchDocs.content: This example shows how to dynamically update resolutions when switching between different video sources.  #include "lib-pid-otrack.h" using namespace DctotrackPID; struct CameraConfig { int model_width, model_height; int display_width, display_height; std::string name; }; void switchCamera(ObjectTrackerLib& tracker, const CameraConfig& config) { printf("Switching to camera: %s\n", config.name.c_str()); printf("Model res: %dx%d, Display res: %dx%d\n", config.model_width, config.model_height, config.display_width, config.display_height); // Update resolutions tracker.ai_obj_trk_set_resolutions( config.model_width, config.model_height, config.display_width, config.display_height ); // Reset PID controllers when switching cameras tracker.ai_obj_trk_reset_pid_controllers(); } int main() { // Define camera configurations CameraConfig cam1 = {640, 384, 1920, 1080, "HD Camera 1"}; CameraConfig cam2 = {320, 192, 1280, 720, "SD Camera 2"}; CameraConfig cam3 = {640, 384, 3840, 2160, "4K Camera 3"}; // Initialize with first camera ObjectTrackerLib tracker( FrameResolution(cam1.model_width, cam1.model_height), FrameResolution(cam1.display_width, cam1.display_height) ); tracker.initializeWithConfig("multi_res_app"); tracker.ai_obj_trk_enable(); CameraConfig* current_cam = &cam1; while (running) { // Check for camera switch if (shouldSwitchCamera()) { CameraConfig* new_cam = selectNewCamera(); switchCamera(tracker, *new_cam); current_cam = new_cam; } // Normal tracking operation std::vector<DetectedObject> detections = getDetections(); tracker.ai_obj_trk_update_detections(detections); PanTiltCommand cmd = tracker.calculatePanTiltCommand(); if (cmd.valid) { controlPTZ(cmd.pan_delta, cmd.tilt_delta); } usleep(33000); } return 0; }

searchDocs.title: Testing M.2 PCIe​
searchDocs.content: In this document, we verify the M.2 PCIe interface using a AP6275P WIFI module.  Plug the module to the M.2 port and follow the steps below.

searchDocs.title: Steps​
searchDocs.content: 1. Generate the WPA Pre-shared Key​  Generating a pre-shared key from a passphrase avoids having to store the passphrase in the WPA Supplicant config file.  From the shell, use the wpa_passphrase command line tool to generate a WPA pre-shared key from a passphrase:  root@sentinel:~# wpa_passphrase network_name 12345678 network={ ssid="network_name" psk=5ba83b0673ea069dafe5d5f1af8216771c13be6ad6f11dac9dc0e90b0c604981 }   2. Bringing up the WLAN Interface​  Use ifconfig to instruct the kernel to bring up the wlan interface:  ifconfig wlan0 up   3. Creating the WPA Supplicant Configuration File​  WPA Supplicant uses a config file to configure the Wifi connection. This configuration file is located in /etc/wpa_supplicant.  Create the /etc/wpa_supplicant directory:  mkdir -p /etc/wpa_supplicant   Create the file /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant-wlan0.conf with options for your Wifi Network.  Contents of an example wpa_supplicant-wlan0.conf:  ctrl_interface=/var/run/wpa_supplicant ctrl_interface_group=0 update_config=1 network={ ssid="network_name" psk=5ba83b0673ea069dafe5d5f1af8216771c13be6ad6f11dac9dc0e90b0c604981 key_mgmt=WPA-PSK scan_ssid=1 }   4. Configure systemd-networkd​  The wlan interface needs to be enabled in the systemd-networkd system daemon configuration.  Create the new file /etc/systemd/network/25-wlan.network with the following contents:  [Match] Name=wlan0 [Network] DHCP=ipv4 DNS=8.8.8.8 DNS=8.8.4.4   5. Enable Wifi Services​  The network daemons need to be restarted to load the new configuration.  Restart network daemons:  systemctl restart systemd-networkd.service systemctl restart wpa_supplicant@wlan0.service   You can enable wpa_supplicant on boot up by  systemctl enable wpa_supplicant@wlan0.service   Use the ifconfig command to verify that wlan0 is enabled.  note If wlan0 does not appear in the ifconfig output, then you may need to run the sync command and reboot. This will make sure that the configuration changes were applied.

searchDocs.title: Image Sensor Cameras​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 includes an integrated ISP and supports connecting image sensor camera modules using the MIPI-CSI connectors. Gstreamer can use these cameras using the V4L2 interface. The ISP supports 3 output paths, the main path supports outputing 4K resolution (if the sensor supports 4K), and the Secondary Paths support 2K resolution. Each path has it’s own video device file in /dev.  The device file number may vary depending on your configuration. You can use the v4l2-ctl command to find which device files are associated with each of the ISP paths.  v4l2-ctl --list-device     An additional video device is created to support Bayer RGB capture. This is the 4th video instance which advertises itself as only supporting Bayer RGB. The other 3 video ports support NV12 / RGB only.  To display video from the ISP’s Main Path:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)60/1' ! waylandsink   To display video from the ISP’s Secondary Paths change the device in the command accordingly.

searchDocs.title: Multi Stream Support​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 supports up to three video streams to be enabled simultaneously (excluding the Bayer RGB video port - vvcam-video.0.3). Up to three different GStreamer pipelines can be run at the same time to validate this feature any combination of up to 3 paths — Main, Secondary Path 1, and Secondary Path 2 can be run simultaneously.  note Although multiple streams may appear as independent devices, all streams originate from a single instance. Once all streams are playing, any change made to an existing stream is treated as a new change. Hence, ensure that all sessions are closed one by one before starting the next set of multi or single streaming.

searchDocs.title: Dual Sensor Support​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 supports dual sensor configuration with the OV5647 sensor module. Dual sensor support required enabling the Sentinel-bothcsi-without-expander.dtbo overlay. (See Updating the ISP Sensor Configuration). Once the two sensors are connected and the overlay is enabled, v4l2-ctl will display a total of eight vvcam-video devices- three NV12 / RGB devices plus one Bayer RGB device per sensor.    Similar to multi stream support, multiple Gstreamer pipelines can be used with both sensors simultaniously.  For example, these commands will display video from the main path of the sensor connected to CSI0 and video from the main path of the sensor connected to CSI1.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video7 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink   note IMX258 and IMX415 sensors are not supported with the dual sensor configuration on Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 boards. Both sensors require a GPIO expander whereas CSI1 is incompatible with the GPIO expander.

searchDocs.title: Updating the ISP Sensor Configuration​
searchDocs.content: By default, Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 is configured to use the OV5647 module with port CSI0. But, the software can be configured to use any of the supported sensor modules. Some configurations require setting a device tree overlay to function correctly. We verified both the CSI0 and CSI1 using OV5647 interface.

searchDocs.title: Steps to verify the CSI interface using OV5647​
Overlays to by used​

searchDocs.title: 1. Updating Device Tree Overlay​
searchDocs.content: Boot into U-Boot by continuosly pressing any key while booting and set variable dtbo with the required device tree overlay.  For example to use the OV5647 camera module in CSI1 port:  setenv dtbo sentinel-sl1680-csi1-without-expander.dtbo   Verify the variable is correctly set in the U-Boot.  printenv   Save the variable to the eMMC for persist in reboot.  saveenv   Finally boot the device with updated overlay.  boot

searchDocs.title: 2. Changing the Camera Sensor Module​
searchDocs.content: The file /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0 is used to display the sensor configuration properties and to update the sensor configuration.  1. Read the current sensor configuration.​  cat /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0   2. Configuring the new module​  Configuring the new module by editing /usr/sbin/isp_media_server.sh script. Change the line which writes the sensor config to /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0. Update the sensor name, xml, and json files for the new sensor.  To list the available xml and json files for sensor please use:  ls /usr/share   For example to use the OV5647 camera module in CSI1 port:    Then restart the isp_media_server service to apply the update.  systemctl restart isp_media_server   3. Getting the camera stream​  We can use the Gstreamer utility for getting the video stream from the camera module.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink   info Please follow the steps to described above to identify the /dev/video device corresponding to the camera module.

searchDocs.title: MIPI-DSI panel configuration parameters​
searchDocs.content: Core Parameters​  Lanes – Number of Data LanesData_Lane_Polarity – Polarity of the Data LaneClk_Lane_Polarity – Polarity of the Clock Lanevirtual_chan – Virtual channel numberVid_mode – Video mode. Supported modes: 0: non-burst mode + sync pulse1: non-burst mode + sync event2: Burst mode non-Continuous_clk – 0 for continuous, 1 for non-continuous clockByte_clk – Byte clock rate = Total Bandwidth / (Lanes × 8)Recv_ack – Receive acknowledgementColor_format – Color coding output format: RGB888 = 5 Loosely_18 – Loosely 18 packed formatData_Polarity – Data enable signal: 0: Positive1: Negative H_polarity – Horizontal polarity active low/HighV_Polarity – Vertical polarityEotp_rx – EOTP Reception enable/disableEotp_tx – EOTP Transmission enable/disable    Timing Parameters​  HTOTAL – Total pixels in a lineChunks – Number of chunks (usually 1)Null_Pkt – Size of the null packetdpi_lp_cmd – Enable DPI low power command    Resolution & Sync​  ACTIVE_WIDTH – Active widthACTIVE_HEIGHT – Active heightHFP – Horizontal Front PorchHSYNCWIDTH – Horizontal Sync WidthHBP – Horizontal Back PorchVFP – Vertical Front PorchVSYNCWIDTH – Vertical Sync WidthVBP – Vertical Back Porch    Format, Scan & Rate​  TYPE – 0 = SD1 = Full HD2 = UHD SCAN – 1 = Progressive0 = Interlaced FRAME_RATE – Frame rate enum values: FRAME_RATE_23P98 = 0 FRAME_RATE_24 = 1 FRAME_RATE_25 = 2 FRAME_RATE_29P97 = 3 FRAME_RATE_30 = 4 FRAME_RATE_47P96 = 5 FRAME_RATE_48 = 6 FRAME_RATE_50 = 7 FRAME_RATE_59P94 = 8 FRAME_RATE_60 = 9 FRAME_RATE_100 = 10 FRAME_RATE_119P88= 11 FRAME_RATE_120 = 12 FRAME_RATE_89P91 = 13 FRAME_RATE_90 = 14     Clock Calculations​  FREQ – Pixel clock frequency (KHz).  Formula:FREQ = HTOTAL × VTOTAL × FRAME_RATE / 1000Example (1080p @ 60Hz):FREQ = 2200 × 1125 × 60 / 1000 = 148500 KHz  PTS_PER_4 – PTS per four count  Formula: (4 × crystal_freq × 1000) / frame_rateExample:PTS_PER_4 = (4 × 90 × 1000) / 60 = 6000  PIXEL_CLOCK – Pixel clock for secondary display, same as FREQ    Power & Initialization​  mipirst-gpio – MIPI reset GPIOpower-supply – External power supply controlbacklight – Backlight controlCOMMAND – Initialization command (hex format)  Command Format:<CMD> <Payload-length-n> <BYTE1> ... <BYTEn>  Long write Ex: 39 04 FF 98 81 03 CMD => 0x39Length => 0x04PayLoad => FF 98 81 0 Delay in microseconds Command format:0xFF <4BYTE delay> Delay for 100ms (100000us => 0x000186A0)FF A0 86 01 00    Display Timing Parameters​  These parameters are mandatory for Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1.  VB_MIN - Minimum vertical blanking for the Display TGHB_MIN - Minimum Horizontal blanking for the Display TGV_OFF - Vertical offset for the Display TG.H_OFF - Horizontal offset for the Display TG.HB_VOP_OFF - Horizontal VOP offset for the Display TG.VB_VOP_OFF - Vertical VOP offset for the Display TG.HB_BE - Horizontal Blanking Back Edge for the Display TG.VB_BE - Vertical Blanking Back Edge for the Display TG.HB_FP - Horizontal Blanking Front porch for the Display TG.VB_FP - Vertical Blanking Front porch for the Display TG.  For reference for a panel with resolution 800x1280 and HTotal = 952, VTOTAL = 1312. Please refer build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/setinel-ws-panel-overlay.dts

searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 integrates many GPIOs to support its various functionalities. This guide will cover how to use GPIOs with Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 and configure their functionality.  On Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1:  All of the GPIOs are multiplexed and can be configured for different functionality. All GPIOs can be assigned interrupts. However, GPO (output only pins) cannot.  Specific details on GPIOs can be found in the Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 Datasheet.

searchDocs.title: GPIO Mappings​
searchDocs.content: GPIO Port	Address	GPIOsgpio0: gpio@2400	f7e82400	0 to 31 gpio1: gpio@0800	f7e80800	32 to 63 gpio2: gpio@0c00	f7e80c00	64 to 95  Userspace GPIO IDs are derived from the gpiochip number, which is dynamically assigned. Modifications to the device configuration, such as updates to the device tree (DTS), can alter the gpiochip number. As a result, userspace GPIO IDs must be recalculated based on the current gpiochip number assigned to the corresponding GPIO controller.  GPIOs 0–31  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + GPIO#  GPIOs 32–63  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + (GPIO# - 32)  GPIOs 64–95  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + (GPIO# - 64)  To do this calculation start by identifying the gpiochip number for the controller on which the GPIO is attached. The address will match the GPIO ports in the tables given. Find which gpiochip is associated with which GPIO port by running ls -l /sys/class/gpio. The symlink will contain the GPIO port address of the port associated with the gpiochip.    The following examples show how to calculate GPIO IDs for various GPIOs, using the gpiochip number associated with the GPIO port.  GPIO 5  GPIO ID = 416 + 5 = 421  GPIO 36  GPIO ID = 480 + (36 - 32) = 484  GPIO 80  GPIO ID = 448 + (80 - 62) = 464

searchDocs.title: Accessing GPIOs from Userspace​
searchDocs.content: GPIOs can be accessed and configured using the GPIO sysfs interface /sys/class/gpio. GPIOs can be exported to userspace and their direction and value can be viewed or set.  For example, to export GPIO[36], run the following steps:  root@setinel:~# echo 484 > /sys/class/gpio/export  Once the GPIO has been exported, the value and direction can be viewed and set:  root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat direction in root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat value 0  By default, the direction is set to input with the value 0. You can modify this by writing to corresponding sysfiles.  root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# echo "out" > direction root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat direction out root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# echo 1 > value root@setinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat value 1

searchDocs.title: Changing the Function of GPIOs​
searchDocs.content: GPIOs assigned for other functinalities can be reconfigured as gpios by updating the device tree entries in the Linux kernel. This requires modifying the linux-dct package using devtool:  Please refer Building workspace section for steps to create a temperory worksapce for development.  Modify the dts file build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts by identifing the current assigned function for the GPIO and reassign them to function as GPIOs.  For example to change the GPIO12,  Identify the functionality of GPIO12  Currently it is configured as UART.   &uart2 { status = "okay"; pinctrl-0 = <&uart2_pmux>; pinctrl-names = "default"; }; uart2_pmux: uart2-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SS2n", "SM_SPI2_SS3n", "SM_SPI2_SDI", "SM_SPI2_SDO"; function = "uart2"; drive-strength = <3>; };   Remove the Pin from the group and add it as another mux node to configure as gpio.  &uart2 { status = "okay"; pinctrl-0 = <&uart2_pmux>; pinctrl-1 = <&uart2gpio_pmux>; pinctrl-names = "default"; };   In &sm_pinctrl node change the following.  uart2_pmux: uart2-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SS2n", "SM_SPI2_SS3n", "SM_SPI2_SDO"; function = "uart2"; drive-strength = <3>; }; uart2gpio_pmux: uart2gpio-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SDI"; function = "gpio"; drive-strength = <7>; };   The pin groups and functions can be found from build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/drivers/pinctrl/berlin/pinctrl-dolphin.c  Please refer Building image section for steps to build the image with updated dts.

searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: This guide explains how to test the HDMI Receiver (RX) interface on the Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1. Follow the steps below to verify HDMI signal integrity, resolution handling, and audio/video passthrough.

searchDocs.title: 1. Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before starting HDMI RX/TX testing, ensure the following:  HDMI source (e.g., laptop, media player).HDMI sink/display (e.g., monitor, TV).Proper HDMI cables (High-Speed recommended).Access to the target board console.

searchDocs.title: 2.1 Connect the HDMI Source​
searchDocs.content: Connect the HDMI source device to the HDMI IN (J9) port of the board.

searchDocs.title: 2.2 Capture Video Stream​
searchDocs.content: Gstreamer can use the V4L2 interface to process and display the video and audio streams received from the external HDMI device.  The V4L2 device file number may vary depending on your configuration. You can use the v4l2-ctl command to find which device files are associated the HDMI-RX device.  v4l2-ctl --list-device

searchDocs.title: Supported Formats​
searchDocs.content: Typical PC Video Formats:​  Format	Bits per Channel	ResolutionRGB	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60 YUV422	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60 YUV444	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60  V4L2 Video Formats:​  Format	ResolutionNV12	4K60 UYVY	4K60  You can use the following commands to route the HDMI RX video to the HDMI sink.  This example displays a 4K30 stream from an external HDMI device using waylandsink:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video6 ! video/x-raw,width=3840,height=2160,fps=30,format=NV12 ! waylandsink fullscreen=true   note For more Gstreamer commands see Gstreamer command line tools

searchDocs.title: 2.3 Check Resolution and Format​
searchDocs.content: Read HDMI input format:  cat /sys/class/drm/card0-HDMI-A-1/modes   Ensure the captured resolution matches the input signal.

searchDocs.title: 2.4 Audio Validation​
searchDocs.content: Audio Formats​  Channels	Sample Rate	Bit Depth2	48kHz	32 bit  Use ALSA utilities for capturing the audio from HDMI-RX:  Use the arecord -l command to determine which ALSA capture device is associated with HDMI-RX.    Use the aplay -l command to determine which ALSA playback device to use to play the captured audio. The following examples will use the speakers associated with the HDMI sink.    After identifying the correct device please run the following command for routing the audio:  gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:0,8 ! queue ! audio/x-raw,format=S32LE,rate=48000,channnels=2 ! alsasink device=hw:0,7 sync=false

searchDocs.title: SD card mode​
searchDocs.content: When SW1 is in ON position, the board will boot in SD card mode. In this mode, the device will load the U-boot stored in the internal SPI flash and will boot up the linux kernel and rootfs present in the SD card. This mode requires an SD card compatible image to be flashed in the SD card which is discussed in thissection. If no SD card is found, the device will stay in the command line of U-boot.

searchDocs.title: eMMC mode​
searchDocs.content: When SW1 is in OFF position, the board will boot in eMMC mode. The device will load the U-boot stored in the eMMC and will further boot up the Linux kernel and rootfs present in eMMC.
