searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: This guide explains how to test the HDMI Transmitter (TX) interface on Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1. Follow the steps below to verify HDMI signal integrity, resolution handling, and audio/video passthrough.

searchDocs.title: 1. Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before starting HDMI RX/TX testing, ensure the following:  HDMI source (e.g., laptop, media player).HDMI sink/display (e.g., monitor, TV).Proper HDMI cables (High-Speed recommended).Access to the target board console.

searchDocs.title: 2. Video sinks available​
searchDocs.content: Gstreamer on Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 supports three video sinks.  The main video sink is the waylandsink which uses the wayland protocol and compositor to display the video output.Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 also supports the DRM KMS sink which displays video frames directly to a Linux DRM device using the kmssink.The xvimagesink is supported when Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 is running an image with the X11 based display server.

searchDocs.title: 2.1 Wayland Sink​
searchDocs.content: Many of the following examples use the Wayland video sink to create a window and render the decoded frames (see GStreamer documentation for more details)  When using the Wayland sink, please make sure to set the following variables in your environment. These variables may need to be set when running commands from the serial console or a remote shell:  export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/var/run/user/0 export WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-1   The XDG_RUNTIME_DIR variable specifies the directory which contains the Wayland socket belonging to the user. The WAYLAND_DISPLAY variable specifies which Wayland compositor to connect to.

searchDocs.title: 2.2 KMS Sink.​
searchDocs.content: The KMS sink supports displaying video without the need to run a windowing system like Wayland, since it can interface directly with Linux DRM devices. (see GStreamer documentation for more details)  Before using kmssink be sure to disable the Wayland service if it is running:  systemctl stop weston.service   You will also need to identify the plane id for the main plane and provide this id to the kmssink element. You can identify the plane id using the modetest command:  modetest -M synaptics   Identify the plane id of the plane which supports formats: NV12 NV21 UYVY VYUY YUYV YVYU

searchDocs.title: 2.3 XvImageSink.​
searchDocs.content: The XvImage sink supports displaying video using the X11 backend. This can be used by, replacing waylandsink with xvimagesink in the Gstreamer commands. (see GStreamer documentation for more details).

searchDocs.title: 3.HDMI configuration​
searchDocs.content: HDMI configuration options in dts are as below:  hdtx-core-config: Used to configure HDMI output, it includes bitfields to control below options.  Default options:hdtx-core-config = /bits/ 8 <1 0 1>  HPD handling: To enable/disable handling of sink hotplug. If HPD handling is disabled, output format will be configured on bootup depending on sink capability and retained till next reboot. HDCP control: To enable/disabled HDCP. Currently not handled. FixedModeset: To let SYNA DRM/KMS driver handle the mode setting internally without exposing user interface. If set, it will configure output format without requiring the userspace application to configure output format, any attempt to override the configured format will be ignored.  hdtx-supported-formats: Used to list the formats exposed to user via kms mode query.  Default selection: hdtx-supported-formats = /bits/ 8 <12 9 10 13 22 21 19 26 25 24 61 62 64>  Refer below file for resolution indices in  build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/drivers/soc/berlin/modules/avio/vpp/ca/include/vpp_defines.h   If needed, this can be overridden using parameter hdmi_preferred_mode, by adding/modifying the same in /etc/modprobe.d/syna_drm.conf.  Example: To override preferred modes as 1080p: hdmi_preferred_mode=1920x1080  Below is out of box default configuration,  syna drm/kms driver will internally configure HDMI output format. On connecting 4K supported sink, 4K30 RGB 8bit format will be selected.On 1080p TV, output will be configured as 1080p60 RGB 8bit. Preferred mode of EDID is override to 1080p.  note For more informations refer general display configuration modes. For HDMI display ID, depending on the capability of the SINK at bootup only 4K or 1080P are supported at present.

searchDocs.title: 4.1 Connect the HDMI Sink​
searchDocs.content: Connect the HDMI sink device to the HDMI OUT/TX (J5) port of the board.

searchDocs.title: 4.2 Verify Signal Detection​
searchDocs.content: On the console, check logs using:  dmesg | grep -i hdmi   or  cat /sys/class/drm/card0-HDMI-A-1/status   Expected output:  connected   Now you can route video to any of the available sinks available using Gstreamer utility (Refer Playing a video file for more commands).  Also the SYNA DRM/KMS driver testing can be done by:  1. Disable Weston  systemctl stop weston.service   2. Identify the plane id for the main plane  modetest -M synaptics   3. Use Modetest tool to route a sample pattern to hdmi-tx  modetest is a tool provided by libdrm library and is available as part of the SDK release/image (/usr/local/bin/modetest). Following are some of the tasks performed with modetest  List all display capabilities: CRTCs, encoders & connectors (DP, HDMI, DSI …), planes, modes…Perform basic tests: display a test pattern, display 2 layers, perform a vsync test.Specify the video mode: resolution and refreshrate.  Below is the syntax.:  modetest -M synaptics -s <connector_id> [, <connector_id>][@<crtc_id>]:[#<mode index>]<mode>[-<vrefresh>][@<format>]   Example: modetest -M synaptics -s 43:1920x1080

searchDocs.title: Connection.​
searchDocs.content: To connect a camera module to the MIPI-CSI connector, use an appropriate CSI FPC flexible cable. If you are using a 15-pin camera module, it can still be connected to the 22-pin CSI0 interface by using a 15-to-22 pin FPC cable. The exact type of cable may vary depending on the camera module, so ensure that the pinout matches and the connection is secure before powering on the system.  The following example shows connecting IMX415 camera module in CSI-0

searchDocs.title: Image Sensor Cameras​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 includes an integrated ISP and supports connecting image sensor camera modules using the MIPI-CSI connectors. Gstreamer can use these cameras using the V4L2 interface. The ISP supports 3 output paths, the main path supports outputing 4K resolution (if the sensor supports 4K), and the Secondary Paths support 2K resolution. Each path has it’s own video device file in /dev.  The device file number may vary depending on your configuration. You can use the v4l2-ctl command to find which device files are associated with each of the ISP paths.  v4l2-ctl --list-device     An additional video device is created to support Bayer RGB capture. This is the 4th video instance which advertises itself as only supporting Bayer RGB. The other 3 video ports support NV12 / RGB only.  To display video from the ISP’s Main Path:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)60/1' ! waylandsink   To display video from the ISP’s Secondary Paths change the device in the command accordingly.  note When using the Wayland sink, please make sure to set the following variables in your environment. export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/var/run/user/0 export WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-1

searchDocs.title: Multi Stream Support​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 supports up to three video streams to be enabled simultaneously (excluding the Bayer RGB video port - vvcam-video.0.3). Up to three different GStreamer pipelines can be run at the same time to validate this feature any combination of up to 3 paths — Main, Secondary Path 1, and Secondary Path 2 can be run simultaneously.  note Although multiple streams may appear as independent devices, all streams originate from a single instance. Once all streams are playing, any change made to an existing stream is treated as a new change. Hence, ensure that all sessions are closed one by one before starting the next set of multi or single streaming.

searchDocs.title: Dual Sensor Support​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 supports dual sensor configuration with the OV5647 sensor module. Dual sensor support required enabling the Sentinel-bothcsi-without-expander.dtbo overlay. (See Updating the ISP Sensor Configuration). Once the two sensors are connected and the overlay is enabled, v4l2-ctl will display a total of eight vvcam-video devices- three NV12 / RGB devices plus one Bayer RGB device per sensor.    Similar to multi stream support, multiple Gstreamer pipelines can be used with both sensors simultaniously.  For example, these commands will display video from the main path of the sensor connected to CSI0 and video from the main path of the sensor connected to CSI1.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video7 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink   note IMX258 and IMX415 sensors are not supported with the dual sensor configuration on Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 boards. Both sensors require a GPIO expander whereas CSI1 is incompatible with the GPIO expander.

searchDocs.title: Updating the ISP Sensor Configuration​
searchDocs.content: By default, Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 is configured to use the OV5647 module with port CSI0. But, the software can be configured to use any of the supported sensor modules. Some configurations require setting a device tree overlay to function correctly. We verified both the CSI0 and CSI1 using OV5647 interface.

searchDocs.title: Steps to verify the CSI interface using OV5647​
Overlays to by used​
searchDocs.content: Sensor	Module	Interface	Device Tree OverlayOV5647	Arducam 5MP OV5647 Camera Module	MIPI-CSI 0 MIPI-CSI 1 Dual CSI0/1	N/A sentinel-sl1680-csi1-without-expander.dtbo sentinel-sl1680-bothcsi-without-expander.dtbo

searchDocs.title: 1. Updating Device Tree Overlay​
searchDocs.content: Boot into U-Boot by continuosly pressing any key while booting and set variable dtbo with the required device tree overlay.  For example to use the OV5647 camera module in CSI1 port:  setenv dtbo sentinel-sl1680-csi1-without-expander.dtbo   Verify the variable is correctly set in the U-Boot.  printenv   Save the variable to the eMMC for persist in reboot.  saveenv   Finally boot the device with updated overlay.  boot

searchDocs.title: 2. Changing the Camera Sensor Module​
searchDocs.content: The file /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0 is used to display the sensor configuration properties and to update the sensor configuration.  1. Read the current sensor configuration.​  cat /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0     2. Configuring the new module​  Configuring the new module by editing /usr/sbin/isp_media_server.sh script. Change the line which writes the sensor config to /proc/vsi/isp_subdev0. Update the sensor name, xml, and json files for the new sensor.  To list the available xml and json files for sensor please use:  ls /usr/share     For example to use the OV5647 camera module in CSI1 port:    Then restart the isp_media_server service to apply the update.  systemctl restart isp_media_server   3. Getting the camera stream​  We can use the Gstreamer utility for getting the video stream from the camera module.  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video3 ! 'video/x-raw, format=(string)NV12, width=(int)640, height=(int)480, framerate=(fraction)30/1' ! waylandsink   info Please follow the steps to described above to identify the /dev/video device corresponding to the camera module.

searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 integrates many GPIOs to support its various functionalities. This guide will cover how to use GPIOs with Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 and configure their functionality.  On Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1:  All of the GPIOs are multiplexed and can be configured for different functionality. All GPIOs can be assigned interrupts. However, GPO (output only pins) cannot.  Specific details on GPIOs can be found in the Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1 Datasheet.

searchDocs.title: GPIO Mappings​
searchDocs.content: GPIO Port	Address	GPIOsgpio0: gpio@2400	f7e82400	0 to 31 gpio1: gpio@0800	f7e80800	32 to 63 gpio2: gpio@0c00	f7e80c00	64 to 95  Userspace GPIO IDs are derived from the gpiochip number, which is dynamically assigned. Modifications to the device configuration, such as updates to the device tree (DTS), can alter the gpiochip number. As a result, userspace GPIO IDs must be recalculated based on the current gpiochip number assigned to the corresponding GPIO controller.  GPIOs 0–31  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + GPIO#  GPIOs 32–63  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + (GPIO# - 32)  GPIOs 64–95  GPIO ID = gpiochip# + (GPIO# - 64)  To do this calculation start by identifying the gpiochip number for the controller on which the GPIO is attached. The address will match the GPIO ports in the tables given. Find which gpiochip is associated with which GPIO port by running ls -l /sys/class/gpio. The symlink will contain the GPIO port address of the port associated with the gpiochip.    The following examples show how to calculate GPIO IDs for various GPIOs, using the gpiochip number associated with the GPIO port.  GPIO 5  GPIO ID = 416 + 5 = 421  GPIO 36  GPIO ID = 480 + (36 - 32) = 484  GPIO 80  GPIO ID = 448 + (80 - 62) = 464

searchDocs.title: Accessing GPIOs from Userspace​
searchDocs.content: GPIOs can be accessed and configured using the GPIO sysfs interface /sys/class/gpio. GPIOs can be exported to userspace and their direction and value can be viewed or set.  For example, to export GPIO[36], run the following steps:  root@sentinel:~# echo 484 > /sys/class/gpio/export  Once the GPIO has been exported, the value and direction can be viewed and set:  root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat direction in root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat value 0  By default, the direction is set to input with the value 0. You can modify this by writing to corresponding sysfiles.  root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# echo "out" > direction root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat direction out root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# echo 1 > value root@sentinel:/sys/class/gpio/gpio484# cat value 1

searchDocs.title: Changing the Function of GPIOs​
searchDocs.content: GPIOs assigned for other functinalities can be reconfigured as gpios by updating the device tree entries in the Linux kernel. This requires modifying the linux-dct package using devtool:  Please refer Building with temporary changes for steps to create a temperory work space for development.  Modify the dts file build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts by identifing the current assigned function for the GPIO and reassign them to function as GPIOs.  For example to change the GPIO12,  Identify the functionality of GPIO12  Currently it is configured as UART.   &uart2 { status = "okay"; pinctrl-0 = <&uart2_pmux>; pinctrl-names = "default"; }; uart2_pmux: uart2-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SS2n", "SM_SPI2_SS3n", "SM_SPI2_SDI", "SM_SPI2_SDO"; function = "uart2"; drive-strength = <3>; };   Remove the Pin from the group and add it as another mux node to configure as gpio.  &uart2 { status = "okay"; pinctrl-0 = <&uart2_pmux>; pinctrl-1 = <&uart2gpio_pmux>; pinctrl-names = "default"; };   In &sm_pinctrl node change the following.  uart2_pmux: uart2-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SS2n", "SM_SPI2_SS3n", "SM_SPI2_SDO"; function = "uart2"; drive-strength = <3>; }; uart2gpio_pmux: uart2gpio-pmux { groups = "SM_SPI2_SDI"; function = "gpio"; drive-strength = <7>; };   The pin groups and functions can be found from build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/drivers/pinctrl/berlin/pinctrl-dolphin.c  Please refer Building image section for steps to build the image with updated dts.

searchDocs.title: Getting Started​
searchDocs.content: This guide explains how to test the HDMI Receiver (RX) interface on the Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1. Follow the steps below to verify HDMI signal integrity, resolution handling, and audio/video passthrough.

searchDocs.title: 1. Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before starting HDMI RX/TX testing, ensure the following:  HDMI source (e.g., laptop, media player).HDMI sink/display (e.g., monitor, TV).Proper HDMI cables (High-Speed recommended).Access to the target board console.

searchDocs.title: 2.1 Connect the HDMI Source​
searchDocs.content: Connect the HDMI source device to the HDMI IN (J9) port of the board.

searchDocs.title: 2.2 Capture Video Stream​
searchDocs.content: Gstreamer can use the V4L2 interface to process and display the video and audio streams received from the external HDMI device.  The V4L2 device file number may vary depending on your configuration. You can use the v4l2-ctl command to find which device files are associated the HDMI-RX device.  v4l2-ctl --list-device

searchDocs.title: Supported Formats​
searchDocs.content: Typical PC Video Formats:​  Format	Bits per Channel	ResolutionRGB	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60 YUV422	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60 YUV444	8, 10, 12 bits	4K60  V4L2 Video Formats:​  Format	ResolutionNV12	4K60 UYVY	4K60  You can use the following commands to route the HDMI RX video to the HDMI sink.  This example displays a 4K30 stream from an external HDMI device using waylandsink:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video7 ! video/x-raw,width=3840,height=2160,fps=30,format=NV12 ! waylandsink fullscreen=true   note When using the Wayland sink, please make sure to set the following variables in your environment. export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/var/run/user/0 export WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-1   note For more Gstreamer commands see Gstreamer command line tools

searchDocs.title: 2.3 Check Resolution and Format​
searchDocs.content: Read HDMI input format:  cat /sys/class/drm/card0-HDMI-A-1/modes   Ensure the captured resolution matches the input signal.

searchDocs.title: 2.4 Audio Validation​
searchDocs.content: Audio Formats​  Channels	Sample Rate	Bit Depth2	48kHz	32 bit  Use ALSA utilities for capturing the audio from HDMI-RX:  Use the arecord -l command to determine which ALSA capture device is associated with HDMI-RX.    Use the aplay -l command to determine which ALSA playback device to use to play the captured audio. The following examples will use the speakers associated with the HDMI sink.    After identifying the correct device please run the following command for routing the audio:  gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:0,8 ! queue ! audio/x-raw,format=S32LE,rate=48000,channels=2 ! alsasink device=hw:0,7 sync=false

searchDocs.title: MIPI-DSI panel configuration parameters​
searchDocs.content: Core Parameters​  Lanes – Number of Data LanesData_Lane_Polarity – Polarity of the Data LaneClk_Lane_Polarity – Polarity of the Clock Lanevirtual_chan – Virtual channel numberVid_mode – Video mode. Supported modes: 0: non-burst mode + sync pulse1: non-burst mode + sync event2: Burst mode non-Continuous_clk – 0 for continuous, 1 for non-continuous clockByte_clk – Byte clock rate = Total Bandwidth / (Lanes × 8)Recv_ack – Receive acknowledgementColor_format – Color coding output format: RGB888 = 5 Loosely_18 – Loosely 18 packed formatData_Polarity – Data enable signal: 0: Positive1: Negative H_polarity – Horizontal polarity active low/HighV_Polarity – Vertical polarityEotp_rx – EOTP Reception enable/disableEotp_tx – EOTP Transmission enable/disable    Timing Parameters​  HTOTAL – Total pixels in a lineChunks – Number of chunks (usually 1)Null_Pkt – Size of the null packetdpi_lp_cmd – Enable DPI low power command    Resolution & Sync​  ACTIVE_WIDTH – Active widthACTIVE_HEIGHT – Active heightHFP – Horizontal Front PorchHSYNCWIDTH – Horizontal Sync WidthHBP – Horizontal Back PorchVFP – Vertical Front PorchVSYNCWIDTH – Vertical Sync WidthVBP – Vertical Back Porch    Format, Scan & Rate​  TYPE – 0 = SD1 = Full HD2 = UHD SCAN – 1 = Progressive0 = Interlaced FRAME_RATE – Frame rate enum values: FRAME_RATE_23P98 = 0 FRAME_RATE_24 = 1 FRAME_RATE_25 = 2 FRAME_RATE_29P97 = 3 FRAME_RATE_30 = 4 FRAME_RATE_47P96 = 5 FRAME_RATE_48 = 6 FRAME_RATE_50 = 7 FRAME_RATE_59P94 = 8 FRAME_RATE_60 = 9 FRAME_RATE_100 = 10 FRAME_RATE_119P88= 11 FRAME_RATE_120 = 12 FRAME_RATE_89P91 = 13 FRAME_RATE_90 = 14     Clock Calculations​  FREQ – Pixel clock frequency (KHz).  Formula:FREQ = HTOTAL × VTOTAL × FRAME_RATE / 1000  Example (1080p @ 60Hz):FREQ = 2200 × 1125 × 60 / 1000 = 148500 KHz  PTS_PER_4 – PTS per four count  Formula: (4 × crystal_freq × 1000) / frame_rate  Example:PTS_PER_4 = (4 × 90 × 1000) / 60 = 6000  PIXEL_CLOCK – Pixel clock for secondary display, same as FREQ    Power & Initialization​  mipirst-gpio – MIPI reset GPIOpower-supply – External power supply controlbacklight – Backlight controlCOMMAND – Initialization command (hex format)  Command Format:<CMD> <Payload-length-n> <BYTE1> ... <BYTEn>  Long write Ex: 39 04 FF 98 81 03 CMD => 0x39Length => 0x04PayLoad => FF 98 81 0 Delay in microseconds Command format:0xFF <4BYTE delay> Delay for 100ms (100000us => 0x000186A0)FF A0 86 01 00    Display Timing Parameters​  These parameters are mandatory for Sentinel SOM_SL1680_Mk1.  VB_MIN - Minimum vertical blanking for the Display TGHB_MIN - Minimum Horizontal blanking for the Display TGV_OFF - Vertical offset for the Display TG.H_OFF - Horizontal offset for the Display TG.HB_VOP_OFF - Horizontal VOP offset for the Display TG.VB_VOP_OFF - Vertical VOP offset for the Display TG.HB_BE - Horizontal Blanking Back Edge for the Display TG.VB_BE - Vertical Blanking Back Edge for the Display TG.HB_FP - Horizontal Blanking Front porch for the Display TG.VB_FP - Vertical Blanking Front porch for the Display TG.  For reference for a panel with resolution 800x1280 and HTotal = 952, VTOTAL = 1312. Please refer build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/setinel-ws-panel-overlay.dts

searchDocs.title: Testing I2C​
searchDocs.content: I2C lines on the 40 pin gpio header can be verified by interfacing with any I2C slave device. In this document, we use a ADS1115 16 Bit ADC 4 channel Module with Programmable Gain Amplifier for verification.

searchDocs.title: Connection diagram​

searchDocs.title: Steps​
searchDocs.content: Scan the i2c bus 0 with i2cdetect utility.  i2cdetect -y -r 0   And verify the i2c address of the device is shown in the output.    Dump the register values using i2cdump utility.  i2cdump -y 0 0x48     Set and get the register values with i2cset and i2cget utilities.  Example:  To convert a analog value to digital using ADS1115  Connect a 3V to the A0 pin of the module and run the following commands.  i2cset -y 0 0x48 0x01 0x83C1 w i2cget -y 0 0x48 0x00 w   note The register read/write commands are specific to the module. Please refer to the module’s datasheet for detailed information.

searchDocs.title: An overview of Yocto SDK​
searchDocs.content: Yocto Project is an open-source build system and toolset for creating custom Linux distributions for embedded devices. The yocto SDK comprises of layers. Each layer contains code for a specific purpose, it might be board specific or general.  Each layer contains multiple recipes. A recipe is a file that describes how to build a particular software component. In order to change a software source code, you need to edit the recipe file associated with it.

searchDocs.title: Adding changes in SDK for development purpose​
searchDocs.content: Yocto provides a command-line tool called devtool to add as well as modify existing recipes and source code. This way, the developer can make changes to the code temporarily without editing the actual recipe. The usage of devtool can be demonstrated with an example :  Suppose you need to change the model name of the root node in the device tree source from Sentinel_sl1680 RDK toSentinel_board RDK. You will have to modify the recipe associated with the linux source. linux_dctis the recipe that handles the linux source code.  Follow the below procedure to change the model name :  Setup the environment before running the devtool utility:  docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):$(pwd) ghcr.io/synaptics-astra/crops:1.0.0 --workdir=$(pwd) MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment  To prepare the recipe for modifying the source code, run  devtool modify linux-dct After executing this command, a workspace directory will be created inside the <build-dir> folder. The source code for linux kernel will be obtained inside the folder <build-dir>/workspace/sources/linux-dct/  Rename the model in the dts file as below You can build the image from here in two ways, either through bitbake utility or continue with the devtool To build using bitbake, execute the following commands : bitbake -f linux-dct -c compile bitbake -f sentinel-media To build using devtool, execute the following commands : devtool build linux-dct devtool build-image sentinel-media  Run the appropriate image as per your requirement. Here, we used the sentinel-media as an example.  If you are satisfied with testing using devtool, you can go back to compiling from the actual recipe by executing the command  devtool reset linux-dct  This will set bitbake to complile the source code of meta-dctk-sentinel instead of workspace. This method of customizing and building is for development purposes. Next topic guides you to integrate those changes permanently into meta-dctk-sentinel .  note When devtool is active, bitbake overrides the actual recipe and looks into the recipe source in the workspace folder. In order to use the actual recipe present in meta-dctk-sentinel, you must execute the reset command.

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: Once power is available, the board will read firmware, bootloader and kernel from a boot device. The most common boot device used is eMMC and SPI flash. This section describes updating eMMC and SPI flash using usb_tool.  A typical image for SOM_SL1680_Mk1 is a directory SYNAIMG, that contains several subimg files and emmc_part_list, emmc_image_list and emmc_image_list_full. The emmc_part_list describes the GUID Partition Table (GPT) which will be used for the eMMC. The emmc_image_list* files specify which sub image files should be written to which partition on the eMMC.  A typical SYNAIMG folder contains the following files :    SOM_SL1680_Mk1 can be updated by running usb_tool in a host system connected to the machine.

searchDocs.title: Hardware setup​
searchDocs.content: To update via USB you will have to connect a USB cable from the host system to the USB Type-C USB 2.0 port as shown below.

searchDocs.title: Flashing from Linux host​
searchDocs.content: In order to flash via USB, you need to have usb_tool installed in your host system. This can be downloaded from here.  After downloading, copy the image folder (SYNAIMG) into the usb_tool directory.  Pre-built eMMC images can be obtained from Sentinel SDK Releases page.Pre-built SPI images can be obtained from SPI U-boot Releases page.

searchDocs.title: Steps to update eMMC​
searchDocs.content: Ensure the eMMC image is present in the usb-tool directory (named eMMCimg for pre-built or SYNAIMG for custom builds).Run the update_emmc script to begin the eMMC update.

searchDocs.title: Steps to update SPI flash​
searchDocs.content: Copy sl1680 folder from SPI U-boot Releases into the usb_tool folder.Run the update_spi script to begin the spi update.    A binary named astra_update gets executed each time when update_emmc or update_spi is executed. The source code for this binary can be found here.  In order to start the update process, SOM_SL1680_Mk1 board needs to be set in the USB_BOOT mode. To do this, press and hold the USB_BOOT button and reset the board by pressing and releasing the reset button.  note Ensure the USB_BOOT button is pressed long enough after the reset button is released. This is to ensure that the device detects the USB_BOOT mode. Also ensure that the board is in eMMC mode.  After booting into USB Boot mode, U-Boot will automatically flash the eMMC/SPI image from the host onto the SOM_SL1680_Mk1board. The board will automatically reboot when the update is complete.

searchDocs.title: Flashing from a Windows PC​
searchDocs.content: SOM_SL1680_Mk1 board can also be updated through a Windows host PC via usb_tool. A USB driver is required to be installed in the host PC for communicating with the board. For that, install the usb_tool as specified previously.  Inside the Synaptics_WinUSB_Driver directory, right click on SYNA_WinUSB.inf and select install from the dropdown menu.    Click on install in the submenu for installing the driver.    note Installing the Windows driver requires an account with administative privileges. Please contact your System Administrator if you do not have sufficient privileges.  After installing the driver, SOM_SL1680_Mk1 board will show up in Windows Device Manager as “Synaptics IoT: Tools package USB Driver for Synaptics Processors” when operating in USB Boot mode.    note SOM_SL1680_Mk1 board won't be detected by the tool or be displayed in the device manager, if the device is not in USB_Boot mode.  Setup the hardware as discussed above.

searchDocs.title: Adding spidev node in dts​
searchDocs.content: For accessing the SPI from user space we need to add spidev node in dts. Make the following change in build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts.  From 1e07e2bbe94a1af9ed36f1e47bcba62b4d2355fc Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001 From: OpenEmbedded <oe.patch@oe> Date: Fri, 11 Jul 2025 15:06:29 +0530 Subject: [PATCH 2/3] Adding spidev node to access spi from userspace --- arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts | 24 +++++++++++++++++++++- 1 file changed, 23 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-) diff --git a/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts b/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts index a7a4d928437e..c14d88438fea 100644 --- a/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts +++ b/arch/arm64/boot/dts/dct/sentinel-sl1680-rdk.dts @@ -494,7 +494,7 @@ &uart0 { }; &uart2 { - status = "okay"; + status = "disabled"; pinctrl-0 = <&uart2_pmux>; pinctrl-names = "default"; }; @@ -985,3 +985,25 @@ levelshift_en { }; }; }; + +&spi0 { + status = "okay"; + // Enable spidev for chip select 0 + spidev@0 { + compatible = "micron,spi-authenta"; + reg = <0>; // chip select 0 + spi-max-frequency = <50000000>; + status = "okay"; + }; +}; + +&spi1 { + status = "okay"; + // Enable spidev for chip select 0 + spidev@0 { + compatible = "micron,spi-authenta"; + reg = <0>; // chip select 0 + spi-max-frequency = <50000000>; + status = "okay"; + }; +}; -- 2.25.1   This changes will add the spidevX.X node in the /dev so that you can acess the SPI bus with spidev_test tool.  note In order to make changes for Adding spidev node in dts, please follow the instruction in Building with temporary changes for adding changes in SDK for development purpose

searchDocs.title: Adding spidev_test tool to the build image​
searchDocs.content: To include the spidev_test user-space tool in your Yocto image.  Steps:​  Create a new recipe  mkdir -p meta-dctk-sentinel/recipes-tools/spidev-test/files   Copy the source file from the kernel to your recipe  cp build/workspace/sources/linux-dct/tools/spi/spidev_test.c meta-dctk-sentinel/recipes-tools/spidev-test/files/   Create the recipe file spidev-test_1.0.bb  Path: meta-dctk-sentinel/recipes-tools/spidev-test/spidev-test_1.0.bb  DESCRIPTION = "SPI Device Test Tool" LICENSE = "GPL-2.0" LIC_FILES_CHKSUM = "file://${COMMON_LICENSE_DIR}/GPL-2.0-only;md5=801f80980d171dd6425610833a22dbe6" SRC_URI = "file://spidev_test.c" S = "${WORKDIR}" do_compile() { ${CC} ${CFLAGS} ${LDFLAGS} -o spidev_test spidev_test.c } do_install() { install -d ${D}${bindir} install -m 0755 spidev_test ${D}${bindir} }   Include the tool in your image  Add the image in meta-dctk-sentinel/recipes-bsp/images/sentinel-media-oobe.bb.  IMAGE_INSTALL:append = " spidev-test"   Build the image  From docker run the commands  bitbake spidev-test bitbake <your-image-name>   This will install spidev_test to /usr/bin/ in the final image.  note You can also build the spidev_test tool directly from the kernel source instead of creating a separate recipe. Please modify the kernel recipe meta-dctk-sentinel/recipes-kernel/linux/linux-dct_5.15.140.bb

searchDocs.title: SD card mode​
searchDocs.content: When SW1 is in ON position, the board will boot in SD card mode. In this mode, the device will load the U-boot stored in the internal SPI flash and will boot up the linux kernel and rootfs present in the SD card. This mode requires an SD card compatible image to be flashed in the SD card which is discussed in thissection. If no SD card is found, the device will stay in the command line of U-boot.

searchDocs.title: eMMC mode​
searchDocs.content: When SW1 is in OFF position, the board will boot in eMMC mode. The device will load the U-boot stored in the eMMC and will further boot up the Linux kernel and rootfs present in eMMC.

searchDocs.title: TFTP Kernel Boot + NFS RootFS Setup​
searchDocs.content: This section documents the support for TFTP-based kernel loading and NFS-based root filesystem mounting for the Sentinel SOM.

searchDocs.title: 1. Setting Up the Server for NFS RootFS​
searchDocs.content: Pre-requisites​  Install the NFS server package on your Linux host:  sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server   Steps​  Download nfs_srv_setup.sh script from Gerrit to the directory containing your rootfs.subimg.gz and home.subimg.gz.Run the setup script:  sudo ./nfs_srv_setup.sh <rootfs_mountpoint> <nfs_set>   Where:  <rootfs_mountpoint> — directory where the SOM rootfs will be hosted.<nfs_set> — set to y when initializing the NFS server for the first time.  Example:  sudo ./nfs_srv_setup.sh /mnt/rootfs y   note In nfs_srv_setup.sh the subnet is set as 192.168.0.0/16. User can change the subnet as per the need.

searchDocs.title: 2. Setting Up TFTP Boot for the Kernel (Server Side)​
searchDocs.content: Pre-requisites​  Install the TFTP server:  sudo apt install tftpd-hpa   Configure TFTP Server​  Edit /etc/default/tftpd-hpa and add:  TFTP_USERNAME="tftp" TFTP_DIRECTORY="/var/lib/tftpboot" TFTP_ADDRESS=":69" TFTP_OPTIONS="--secure"   Set up TFTP directory​  sudo mkdir -p /srv/tftp sudo chown -R tftp:tftp /srv/tftp sudo chmod -R 755 /srv/tftp   Restart service:  sudo systemctl restart tftpd-hpa   Copy Kernel Boot Image​  Copy boot.subimg from SYNAIMG to the TFTP directory:  cp boot.subimg /srv/tftp/

searchDocs.title: 3. Setting Up TFTP Boot on the SOM (Client Side)​
searchDocs.content: Configure Network in U-Boot​  In the U-Boot console:  setenv serverip <tftp_server_ip> setenv ipaddr <som_ip_address> saveenv   Boot Using TFTP​  netboot <start_address> <dtb_offset> <file_name>   Where:  <start_address> — recommended: 0x20000000<dtb_offset> — offset of the DTB inside boot.subimg<file_name> — TFTP-available boot image filename  Extract DTB offset:  binwalk boot.subimg | grep "Flattened device tree" | awk '{print $2}'   note In astra SDK 1.8.0 instead of using the netboot command please use the fillowing command: tftpboot 0x20000000 boot.subimg bootram 0x20000000

searchDocs.title: 4. Setting NFS RootFS on SOM​
searchDocs.content: To boot kernel with NFS rootfs, configure two variables in U‑Boot.  1. Enable Bootargs Override​  setenv bootargscontrol y   2. Set Bootargs for NFS RootFS​  setenv bootargs 'console=ttyS0,115200 root=/dev/nfs nfsroot=<nfs_server_ip>:<nfs_rootfs_folder>,nfsvers=3,tcp,rw ip=<som_ip>:<server_ip>:<gateway_ip>:<netmask>::eth0:off'   Example:  setenv bootargs 'console=ttyS0,115200 root=/dev/nfs \ nfsroot=192.168.1.102:/mnt/rootfs,nfsvers=3,tcp,rw \ ip=192.168.1.110:192.168.1.102:192.168.1.1:255.255.0.0::eth0:off'   By default, bootargs normally point to the SD card partitions. Setting the above overrides them for NFS boot.

searchDocs.title: Creating a bootable SD card image​
searchDocs.content: An existing image(SYNAIMG/eMMCimg) can be converted into a bootable SD card image. Follow the below steps to create a bootable SD card image :  Download gen_sd.sh script from Github and paste it in the image folder (SYNAIMG/eMMCimg). The script runs in a Linux environment with the mkfs.ext4, gzip, gdisk, and sgdisk utilties installed. Make the file executable and run it from within the image folder  chmod a+x gen_sd.sh ./gen_sd.sh  If the script executes successfully as shown below, an output file SD.img is created. This is the bootable image to be flashed in the SD card.    Flash the bootable image into the SD card using balena etcher tool.  When balena etcher is open, select the SD.img created inside the image folder. After inserting the SD card into the host PC, select the SD card from the storage option. Then click the flash option. The image will get flashed. If flashing is successful, a success message will be displayed as shown.  note It may take about 10 - 20 minutes to flash the image into the SD card. This time depends on the speed of SD card and the host machine.  After flashing, insert the SD card into the SD slot as shown below and boot the device in SD card mode.

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: This page describes the steps to build Yocto images for SOM_SL1680_Mk1 and EVK_SL1680_Mk1. This guide assumes that the reader already has some familiarity with Yocto concepts. If not please refer Yocto documentation for a quick overview.

searchDocs.title: Building the image​
searchDocs.content: To ensure proper configuration and clean environment, the build must be performed inside a docker container. Synaptics provides a pre-built container at ghcr.io/synaptics-astra/crops. To start the container, execute the command :  docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):$(pwd) -v ~/.ssh/:/home/pokyuser/.ssh ghcr.io/synaptics-astra/crops:1.0.0 --workdir=$(pwd)   -v ~/.ssh/:/home/pokyuser/.ssh parameter must be added to let the container access the ssh keys in the system for cloning private repositories for recipes. In order to do so, you must ensure your system has access rights to the private repository.  If SW 1.0.3 or higher version is used, start the container using this command :  docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):$(pwd) -v ~/.ssh/:/home/pokyuser/.ssh ghcr.io/synaptics-astra/crops:1.1.0 --workdir=$(pwd)   note On Ubuntu 20 and 18 LTS, the seccomp protection feature of Docker has to be disabled when creating the build container by adding the parameter --security-opt "seccomp=unconfined" after the --rm parameter in the docker command.  To build sentinel-media image, execute the following commands from the sdk directory  MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment bitbake sentinel-media  To build sentinel-media-oobe image, execute the following commands from the sdk directory  OOBE=enabled MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment bitbake sentinel-media-oobe  This creates a default folder named build in the sdk directory. You can also specify the name of your build directory by passing it as an argument in the setup command. For example to create the build folder as build-sentinel, modify the command as :  MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment build-sentinel  The build folder will be the parent directory where yocto does its compilations and provide the final image. The final image after the build process will be found in <build-dir>/tmp/deploy/images/sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1/SYNAIMG/  If you are rebuilding the same image for the same machine, it is recommended to clean the generated build artifacts of the image before rebuilding. In order to clean, execute the command :  bitbake -c clean <image-name>  note The SDK is based on Synaptics' Astra SDK which is implemented for their Astra Machina Series. The Sentinel series uses the same SOC (SL1680) as Synaptics with some modifications. So, we will have to use Synaptics' SDK for full functionalities. For this, you must accept the End User License Agreement of Synaptics while setting up the environment to build the yocto image.

searchDocs.title: Adding Distro features​
searchDocs.content: Sentinel Yocto SDK supports optional distribution features which can be enabled either in <build-dir>/conf/local.conffile or by passing variables to the setup-environment script.

searchDocs.title: X11 Display server​
searchDocs.content: In Sentinel SDK, Wayland is the default display server. You can set the display server to X11 by passing DISPLAY_SERVERvariable to the setup-environment script.  MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 DISPLAY_SERVER=x11 source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment

searchDocs.title: Virtualization for OOBE​
searchDocs.content: Virtualization feature is added to enable the support for virtual machines and containers. To enable virtualization and OOBE support, you need to pass the OOBE variable to the setup-environment script.  MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 OOBE=enabled source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment

searchDocs.title: Image selection​
searchDocs.content: The user will have to select the class of images he/she is going to use before building an image. The IMAGE_CLASS variable is used to specify the class of images while setting up the environment.  For example, the below command allow users to build the images that belong to the sentinel image class.  MACHINE=sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1-rfb-mk1 OOBE=enabled IMAGE_CLASS=sentinel source meta-dctk-sentinel/setup/setup-environment  note If the user is not providing the IMAGE_CLASS variable, then yocto by default selects the sentinel class.  The following are the image classes into which the images are packed :  Image Class	Imagessentinel	sentinel-media-oobe, sentinel-media

searchDocs.title: Prerequisites​
searchDocs.content: Before building the Object Detection plugin, you need to set up the toolchain for Sentinel SoM. Refer to the Toolchain for Sentinel SoM documentation for detailed instructions on obtaining and activating the toolchain.  Once the toolchain is installed, activate it by sourcing the environment setup script:  source /opt/poky/4.0.17/environment-setup-cortexa73-poky-linux

searchDocs.title: Build Options​
searchDocs.content: The Object Detection plugin supports multiple inference backends through the MACH build option:  MACH_SYNAP - SyNAP framework (hardware accelerated, default for cross-compilation)  The build system automatically selects the appropriate backend:  Cross-compilation (for Sentinel SoM): Defaults to MACH_SYNAP

searchDocs.title: Building with SyNAP Backend​
searchDocs.content: To build with SyNAP framework support (default for cross-compilation):  rm -rf builddir/ export SYNAP_FRAMEWORK_PATH=/path/to/synap/framework meson setup builddir -DMACH=SYNAP ninja -C builddir   Or specify the SyNAP path via build option:  meson setup builddir -DMACH=SYNAP -Dsynap_framework_path=/path/to/synap/framework ninja -C builddir   note The SYNAP_FRAMEWORK_PATH environment variable or synap_framework_path option must be set when building with MACH_SYNAP.  note The build process will automatically link against the required GStreamer libraries and the selected inference backend if they are properly configured in the toolchain environment.

searchDocs.title: Deploying to the Board​
searchDocs.content: After building the plugin, push it to the Sentinel board using ADB:  adb push builddir/libgstdctobd.so /usr/lib/gstreamer-1.0/

searchDocs.title: Verification​
searchDocs.content: Connect to the board shell and verify the plugin installation:  adb shell gst-inspect-1.0 dctobd | col -b   If the plugin is installed correctly, you will see the element properties and capabilities listed in the output.

searchDocs.title: Project Structure​
searchDocs.content: The Object Detection plugin source code follows a three-layer architecture:  object_detection/ ├── inc/ │ ├── api/ # API layer (C interface) │ │ └── apidctobd.h # Public API header │ ├── gst/ # GStreamer layer │ │ ├── gstdctobdinfer.h # Inference element │ │ ├── gstdctdctobdsink.h # Sink element │ │ └── gstdctobdmeta.h # Metadata definitions │ └── mach/ # Machine layer (inference backends) │ ├── mach_dctobd.h # Backend abstraction │ ├── mach_synap.h # SyNAP interface ├── src/ │ ├── api/ # API implementation │ │ └── apidctobd.c │ ├── gst/ # GStreamer implementation │ │ ├── gstdctobdinfer.cpp │ │ ├── gstdctdctobdsink.cpp │ │ ├── gstdctobdmeta.cpp │ │ └── gstdctobdplugin.cpp │ └── mach/ # Backend implementations │ ├── mach_synap.cpp # SyNAP implementation ├── test/ # Test applications ├── meson.build # Build configuration └── meson_options.txt # Build options

searchDocs.title: Testing​
searchDocs.content: The plugin provides test applications in the test/ directory to demonstrate plugin functionality.  To build the test applications along with the plugin, execute:  meson compile -C builddir   After building, run the test application with:  ./builddir/test/test_dctobd_api   note Make sure to configure the model path and video source in the test application before running.

searchDocs.title: Debugging​
searchDocs.content: To enable detailed debug output from the plugin, set the GST_DEBUG environment variable before running the pipeline:  export GST_DEBUG=dctobd:5   After setting the debug level, run your pipeline to see detailed log messages:  GST_DEBUG=dctobd:5 gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobdmodel=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector output=json ! dctobdsink location=output.txt   Debug levels range from 0 (no output) to 5 (verbose logging). Level 5 provides the most detailed information for troubleshooting.  note If you encounter issues with the plugin, verify that all dependencies are properly installed and that the model file path is correct.

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: This guide describes the steps to set up the source code and install dependencies for building an image.  Sentinel BSP works with the Yocto Kirkstone release and provides support for SOM_SL1680_Mk1 under the machine name sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1. The supported images for sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1 are :  Image Name	Descriptionsentinel-core	Core system packages intended for power management testing. sentinel-media	Default image which contains core packages along with full packages supporting multimedia capabilities. sentinel-media-oobe	Contains all packages in sentinel-media, along with Chromium, Docker, development tools, and demo apps.

searchDocs.title: Installing the Yocto source​
searchDocs.content: Before installing the source code, you must have repo utility and git installed in your system. Follow the below steps to configure repo and git in your system.  Install curl using the command :  sudo apt install curl   Install repo utility using the following commands :  mkdir -p ~/bin PATH=~/bin:$PATH curl https://storage.googleapis.com/git-repo-downloads/repo > ~/bin/repo chmod a+x ~/bin/repo   Install and configure git in your system if its not present, using the following commands :  sudo apt install git git config --global user.name <your-username> git config --global user.email <your-email-id>   Execute the following commands to clone the bsp layer of sentinel-som-sl1680-mk1 based on the firmware version:  mkdir ~/sdk && cd ~/sdk repo init -u git@github.com:dicortech/sentinel-utils -m manifests/manifest_v1.0.3.xml -b public_v1.x.x repo sync -j4

searchDocs.title: Build host requirements​
searchDocs.content: The recommended hardware is an x86_64 host with at least:  16 cores32 GB of RAM150 GB of disk  The recommended software configuration is the following:  Ubuntu 24.04 LTSDocker 20.10 or later provided by the standard Ubuntu package docker.io  Other versions of Linux and Docker may also work but may need special configuration.

searchDocs.title: Docker Setup​
searchDocs.content: If docker is not installed in your device, please follow the below installation instructions :  Install docker package :  sudo apt install docker.io   Add the current user to the docker group to use docker :  sudo adduser ${USER} docker   To apply the changes to the current shell you can also run the following commands :  newgrp docker newgrp ${USER}

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: The Object Detection Plugin provides two GStreamer elements that work together to perform real-time object detection on video streams:  1. dctobd (Object Detection Transform Element)  The dctobd element performs object detection inference on incoming video frames. It accepts RGB video input, runs the detection model, and outputs the video frames with detection metadata attached.  2. dctobdsink (Object Detection Sink Element)  The dctobdsink element writes detection results to a file. It can output results in JSON format or attach overlay metadata for rendering.

searchDocs.title: Key Features​
searchDocs.content: Model Management - Dynamic model selection and directory scanningDetection Control - Enable/disable detection at runtimeClass Filtering - Select specific object classes to detectThreshold Control - Adjust confidence threshold dynamicallyInference Statistics - Optional performance monitoring

searchDocs.title: Architecture​
searchDocs.content: The plugin follows a three-layer architecture for modularity and maintainability:

searchDocs.title: 1. API Layer (inc/api/, src/api/)​
searchDocs.content: Provides a clean, high-level C API for applications with functions like:  api_dctobd_set_model() - Set model file pathapi_dctobd_set_confidence_threshold() - Configure detection thresholdapi_dctobd_set_enabled_classes() - Filter specific object classes

searchDocs.title: 2. GStreamer Layer (inc/gst/, src/gst/)​
searchDocs.content: Handles GStreamer plugin implementation:  Pipeline integration and caps negotiationProperty managementBuffer processing and metadata attachment

searchDocs.title: 3. Machine Layer (inc/mach/, src/mach/)​
searchDocs.content: Platform-specific inference implementation:  SyNAP (mach_synap.cpp) - Hardware-accelerated neural network operations

searchDocs.title: Quick Start​
searchDocs.content: To run object detection on a video stream, use the following command:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=results.txt   note Ensure that the video format is set to RGB and the resolution matches your model's input size before passing it to the dctobd element.

searchDocs.title: Supported Input Formats​
searchDocs.content: Video Format: RGB only (use videoconvert for other formats)Resolution: Must match the model's expected input dimensionsColor Space: Standard RGB color space

searchDocs.title: Requirements​
searchDocs.content: To use the Object Detection Plugin, you will need the following dependencies installed on Sentinel SoM:

searchDocs.title: For SyNAP Backend (MACH_SYNAP)​
searchDocs.content: GStreamer 1.0 development librariesSynaptics SyNAP framework libraries (synap_app, synap_base, synap_utils, synap_img, synapnb, synap_preprocess, synap_postprocess)Pre-trained object detection model (.synap format)

searchDocs.title: Updating eMMC from U-boot​
searchDocs.content: Both instances of U-boot allows flashing image into eMMC. The image can be obtained from a USB device connected to any USB interfaces or through ethernet. In order to access the U-boot prompt, you must have access to the device's serial console. To use the serial console, refer Debug console access.    To access the U-boot prompt, you will have to interrupt the normal boot process by typing any keys into the serial console. If the U-boot console is active you will see a symbol(=>) at the leftmost portion of a line. The U-boot instance(eMMC/SPI) loaded into the memory depends on the mode in which the device is set.  If the device is in eMMC mode, then the U-boot from eMMC is loaded.If the device is in SD card mode, then the U-boot from internal SPI flash is loaded.  You can find more about modes here.

searchDocs.title: Flashing from USB drive​
searchDocs.content: To flash an image from USB drive, copy the image directory (SYNAIMG) into the USB drive. The drive must have a partition with FAT32 formatted filesystem and can be connected to any of the USB ports.  Flash the image into eMMC using the command :  => usb2emmc SYNAIMG  If the flashing operation is successful, you will get a log similar to this :

searchDocs.title: Flashing images from TFTP server​
searchDocs.content: To flash an eMMC image from a TFTP server, you must connect SOM_SL1680_Mk1 board to a network where a tftp server is running via its ethernet port. Ensure a valid eMMC image is present in the tftp server. Once device is connected to the network, boot the device to its U-boot prompt.  Initialize the network configurations in the device my executing the following commands :  => net_init; => setenv serverip <ip-address-of-tftp-server> => setenv ipaddr <ip-address of device>  After setting the network configuration, to flash the eMMC, execute the command :  => tftp2emmc SYNAIMG    If flashing operation is successful, the following log will be received :

searchDocs.title: Updating internal SPI flash from U-boot​
searchDocs.content: You can also update the internal SPI flash of device from the loaded U-boot. Latest SPI images for U-boot can be obtained fromGithub.

searchDocs.title: Flashing from USB drive​
searchDocs.content: Copy the SPI U-boot image into a USB drive that has a FAT32 formatted filesystem. Execute the following commands in U-boot terminal :  => usb start; fatload usb 0 0x10000000 spi_uboot_en_sl1680_dct_20250305.bin; => spinit; => erase f0000000 f01fffff; cp.b 0x10000000 0xf0000000 0x200000;

searchDocs.title: Flashing from TFTP server​
searchDocs.content: Copy the SPI U-boot image into the tftp server. In U-boot, you need to initialize the network for fetching the image from tftp server. Execute the following commands to setup network and flash image :  => net_init; => setenv serverip <ip-address of tftp server> => setenv ipaddr <ip-address of device> => tftpboot 0x10000000 <U-boot_image_name>; => spinit; => erase f0000000 f01fffff; cp.b 0x10000000 0xf0000000 0x200000;    note Ensure that the device and the server are in the same network. <ip-address of device> can be any address that comes under the netmask of tftp server.  In both flashing methods, an optional backup copy of the SPI flash image can be installed using the command:  => erase f0000000 f01fffff; cp.b 0x10000000 0xf0000000 0x200000;  note If the U-boot is loaded from the internal SPI flash, net_init command will be disabled as the U-boot will automatically initialize the network.

searchDocs.title: Required Pipeline Elements​
searchDocs.content: For proper operation, your pipeline should include:  videoconvert - Converts any video format (YUV, NV12, BGRA, etc.) to RGBvideoscale - Resizes video to match model's expected resolutionCaps filter - Explicitly specify video/x-raw,format=RGB,width=W,height=H  Example pipeline structure:  [source] ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,format=RGB,width=640,height=384 ! \ dctobd model=/path/to/model.synap mode=detector ! \ [sink]

searchDocs.title: Basic Detection​
searchDocs.content: To run object detection with default settings, execute the following pipeline:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=results.txt   This pipeline captures video from /dev/video8, converts it to RGB format, and runs object detection. Results are written to results.txt in JSON format.

searchDocs.title: Class-Specific Detection​
searchDocs.content: To detect only specific object classes, use the enabled-classes property:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector enabled-classes="person,car,bicycle" frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=results.txt   This configuration will only detect persons, cars, and bicycles, ignoring all other object classes.

searchDocs.title: Adjusting Detection Threshold​
searchDocs.content: To use a higher confidence threshold for more accurate detections, set the threshold property:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector threshold=0.75 frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=results.txt   A threshold of 0.75 means only detections with 75% or higher confidence will be reported.

searchDocs.title: Application Examples​
searchDocs.content: The following examples demonstrate how to use the Object Detection plugin in C applications.

searchDocs.title: Configuring Detection at Runtime​
searchDocs.content: GstElement *dctobd = gst_element_factory_make("dctobd", "detector"); // Set the model path g_object_set(dctobd, "model", "/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap", NULL); // Configure detection parameters g_object_set(dctobd, "mode", "detector", NULL); g_object_set(dctobd, "enabled-classes", "person,car", NULL); g_object_set(dctobd, "threshold", 0.7f, NULL);

searchDocs.title: Querying Available Classes​
searchDocs.content: // After the model is loaded, query available classes gchar *available_classes = NULL; g_object_get(dctobd, "available-classes", &available_classes, NULL); g_print("Available classes: %s\n", available_classes); g_free(available_classes);

searchDocs.title: Person Detection​
searchDocs.content: This configuration optimizes for detecting people with high confidence:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector enabled-classes="person" threshold=0.7 frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=person_detection.txt

searchDocs.title: Vehicle Detection​
searchDocs.content: This configuration detects multiple vehicle types:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector enabled-classes="car,truck,bus,motorcycle" threshold=0.6 frameinterval=5 ! \ dctobdsink location=vehicle_detection.txt   note Adjust the frameinterval parameter based on your performance requirements. Higher values reduce CPU usage but may miss rapid changes in the scene.

searchDocs.title: Video File Input​
searchDocs.content: gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location=video.mp4 ! decodebin ! \ videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,format=RGB,width=640,height=384 ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector frameinterval=3 ! \ fakesink

searchDocs.title: RTSP Stream Input​
searchDocs.content: gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location=rtsp://camera_ip/stream ! \ rtph264depay ! h264parse ! decodebin ! \ videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,format=RGB,width=640,height=384 ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector frameinterval=3 ! \ fakesink

searchDocs.title: Enable Debug Logging​
searchDocs.content: To see detailed plugin logs, set the GST_DEBUG environment variable:  # Show only DCTOBD plugin debug messages (recommended) GST_DEBUG=dctobd:4,dctobdsink:4 gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=/tmp/results.txt # Show all GStreamer debug messages (very verbose) GST_DEBUG=*:3 gst-launch-1.0 ...   Debug levels:  0: No output1: ERROR2: WARNING3: INFO4: DEBUG5: LOG (verbose)

searchDocs.title: Enable Inference Statistics​
searchDocs.content: Monitor inference performance:  gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video8 ! videoconvert ! videoscale ! \ video/x-raw,width=640,height=384,format=RGB ! \ dctobd model=/usr/share/synap/models/object_detection/coco/model/yolov8s-640x384/model.synap \ mode=detector inferstatistics=true frameinterval=3 ! \ dctobdsink location=results.txt   This will log average inference time when the pipeline stops.

searchDocs.title: Dynamic Property Changes​
searchDocs.content: You can change detection parameters at runtime using GStreamer's property system:  GstElement *dctobd = gst_element_factory_make("dctobd", "detector"); // Start with person detection g_object_set(dctobd, "enabled-classes", "person", NULL); g_object_set(dctobd, "threshold", 0.7f, NULL); // Run pipeline... gst_element_set_state(pipeline, GST_STATE_PLAYING); // Later, switch to vehicle detection g_object_set(dctobd, "enabled-classes", "car,truck,bus,motorcycle", NULL); g_object_set(dctobd, "threshold", 0.6f, NULL); // Temporarily disable detection g_object_set(dctobd, "detection-enabled", FALSE, NULL); // Re-enable with new settings g_object_set(dctobd, "detection-enabled", TRUE, NULL); g_object_set(dctobd, "threshold", 0.8f, NULL);

searchDocs.title: Issue: "Unsupported video format" Error​
searchDocs.content: Cause: The plugin only accepts RGB format input.  Solution: Add videoconvert before the dctobd element:  ... ! videoconvert ! video/x-raw,format=RGB ! dctobd...

searchDocs.title: Issue: "Resolution mismatch" Error​
searchDocs.content: Cause: Video resolution doesn't match model's expected input.  Solution: Add videoscale and specify correct resolution:  ... ! videoscale ! video/x-raw,format=RGB,width=640,height=384 ! dctobd...

searchDocs.title: Issue: No Detections Appearing​
searchDocs.content: Possible Solutions:  Lower the threshold: threshold=0.3Check detection is enabled: detection-enabled=trueVerify enabled classes match scene objectsCheck frame interval isn't too highEnable debug logging to see format/resolution info

searchDocs.title: Issue: Class Filtering Not Working​
searchDocs.content: Possible Solutions:  Ensure label file exists (set via label property)Check class name spelling and case sensitivityQuery available classes first:  gchar *available = NULL; g_object_get(dctobd, "available-classes", &available, NULL); g_print("Available: %s\n", available); g_free(available);

searchDocs.title: Architecture​
searchDocs.content: The plugin library is organized into different layers.  GST Layer - The GST layer has the main Gstreamer related functionalities. However, the functional tasks which can be offloaded to different hardware is kept in the machine layer. Machine Layer - This is the layer where machine specific operations are implemented. This is done to port the plugin easily to different platforms. Currently supports JSON parsing with extensibility for Protocol Buffers and other formats. Communication Layer - This layer handles the communication of the plugin to the external world. It publishes tracking results via MQTT or other protocols. API Layer - The API layer is a wrapper layer using which the user can configure the gstreamer plugin. This is not part of the gstreamer framework. Instead of the API layer, the user can use gstreamer's APIs directly too.

searchDocs.title: Folder Structure​
searchDocs.content: The corresponding folder structure is as follows:  inc/ # Header files ├── gst/ # GStreamer layer (plugin interface) ├── mach/ # Machine layer (detection parsing) ├── comm/ # Communication layer (MQTT integration) ├── api/ # API layer (C interface) └── lib/ # ByteTrack library (tracking algorithms) src/ # Source files ├── gst/ # GStreamer implementation ├── mach/ # Machine implementations (json parser, etc.) ├── comm/ # Communication implementation (MQTT) ├── api/ # API implementation └── lib/ # ByteTrack algorithm implementation test/ # Test applications ├── test_dctotrack.c # Basic GStreamer pipeline test └── api/ └── test_api_dctotrack.c # API-based test application

searchDocs.title: Plugin Elements​
searchDocs.content: This plugin provides one GStreamer element:

searchDocs.title: dctotrack (Detection to Tracking Transform)​
searchDocs.content: Transform element that performs multi-object tracking on incoming video frames with detection metadata. It accepts video frames with detection results attached as metadata, runs the ByteTrack algorithm, and outputs the video frames with tracking results.  Capabilities:  Input: video/x-raw with detection metadataOutput: video/x-raw with tracking results

searchDocs.title: Features​
searchDocs.content: This gstreamer plugin has the following features/functionalities:

searchDocs.title: Tracking Algorithm​
searchDocs.content: ByteTrack Implementation: State-of-the-art multi-object tracking algorithmKalman filtering for motion predictionIoU (Intersection over Union) based data associationLinear Assignment Problem (LAPJV) solver for optimal matchingFour-state track management (New, Tracked, Lost, Removed)

searchDocs.title: Detection Integration​
searchDocs.content: Metadata Processing: Seamless integration with DCTOBD detection pluginJSON-based detection data parsingSupport for normalized and pixel coordinatesExtensible for Protocol Buffers and other formats

searchDocs.title: Tracking Control​
searchDocs.content: Configurable Thresholds: Track threshold (minimum confidence to start tracking)High threshold for first associationIoU match threshold for track-detection matchingTrack buffer (frames to keep lost tracks)Frame rate configuration for motion prediction

searchDocs.title: Output Modes​
searchDocs.content: Flexible Output Options: None: Silent tracking (no output)Text: Human-readable JSON to stdoutMQTT: Real-time publishing to MQTT brokerBoth: Text + MQTT simultaneously

searchDocs.title: Output Formats​

searchDocs.title: Overview​
searchDocs.content: The STT Plugin provides a GStreamer sink element (dctstt) that performs real-time speech-to-text conversion on audio streams. It accepts 16kHz mono PCM audio input, runs either Vosk or Whisper speech recognition models, and outputs recognition results through multiple communication backends.  dctstt (Speech-to-Text Sink Element)  The dctstt element is a sink element that terminates an audio pipeline. It accepts audio input, performs speech recognition using either Vosk (S16LE format) or Whisper (F32LE format), and outputs text results through TCP, MQTT, or console output.

searchDocs.title: Key Features​
searchDocs.content: Offline Speech Recognition - No internet connection required, all processing happens locallyDual Engine Support - Vosk for lightweight recognition or Whisper for higher accuracy (compile-time selection)Multiple Communication Backends - TCP JSON server, MQTT publishing, or console output (compile-time selection)Partial Results Support - Real-time streaming of partial recognition results during speech (Vosk only)Grammar Support - Can be configured with custom grammar for improved accuracy on specific vocabulary (Vosk)Voice Activity Detection - Built-in VAD for efficient processing (Whisper only)GStreamer Integration - Standard GStreamer element properties and bus messagesMulti-language Support - Support for multiple languages through different models

searchDocs.title: Architecture​
searchDocs.content: The STT plugin follows a three-layer architecture for modularity and maintainability:

searchDocs.title: 1. GStreamer Layer (gstdctstt.cpp)​
searchDocs.content: Handles GStreamer plugin implementation:  Pipeline integration and audio buffer processingProperty management (model path, communication settings, engine-specific options)Bus message posting for recognition resultsSink pad for receiving audio data

searchDocs.title: 2. Speech Recognition Engine Layer​
searchDocs.content: Two engines are available (compile-time selection):  Vosk Integration:  Vosk API - Lightweight offline speech recognitionSupports S16LE audio format (16-bit PCM)Model loading from directory structureReal-time partial results supportJSON result parsing  Whisper Integration:  Whisper.cpp - Higher accuracy offline speech recognitionSupports F32LE audio format (32-bit float PCM)Model loading from GGML binary filesBuilt-in Voice Activity Detection (VAD)Configurable processing parameters (threads, step-ms, length-ms)

searchDocs.title: 3. Communication Layer (com/)​
searchDocs.content: Platform-specific output implementation with three backends:  TCP (comm_tcp.cpp) - JSON server on configurable portMQTT (comm_mqtt.cpp) - Publish results to MQTT brokerPrintf (comm_printf.cpp) - Console output for debugging  info Both the speech recognition engine and communication backend are selected at compile-time using build options. Only one engine and one backend are compiled into the plugin at a time.

searchDocs.title: Using Vosk (S16LE format)​
searchDocs.content: gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! \ audioconvert ! \ audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=S16LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15

searchDocs.title: Using Whisper (F32LE format)​
searchDocs.content: gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! \ audioconvert ! \ audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=F32LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/whisper/ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin   note Audio Format Requirements: Vosk: S16LE (16-bit signed PCM), 1 channel, 16000 HzWhisper: F32LE (32-bit float PCM), 1 channel, 16000 Hz Use audioconvert and audioresample to convert from other formats.

searchDocs.title: Vosk Engine​
searchDocs.content: Audio Format: S16LE (16-bit signed little-endian PCM)Sample Rate: 16000 HzChannels: 1 (mono)Layout: Interleaved

searchDocs.title: Whisper Engine​
searchDocs.content: Audio Format: F32LE (32-bit float little-endian PCM)Sample Rate: 16000 HzChannels: 1 (mono)Layout: Interleaved  tip Use audioconvert and audioresample to convert stereo or different format audio to the required format for your chosen engine.

searchDocs.title: Requirements​
searchDocs.content: To use the STT Plugin, you will need the following dependencies installed on Sentinel SoM:

searchDocs.title: Runtime Dependencies​
searchDocs.content: GStreamer 1.0 runtime librariesALSA libraries (for audio capture)  For Vosk Engine:  Vosk library (libvosk.so) version 0.3.45 or compatiblePre-trained Vosk speech recognition model (directory structure)  For Whisper Engine:  Whisper.cpp libraryPre-trained Whisper model in GGML format (.bin file)

searchDocs.title: Communication Backend Dependencies​
searchDocs.content: Depending on the compiled backend:  TCP Backend: No additional dependenciesMQTT Backend: libmosquitto (MQTT client library)Printf Backend: No additional dependencies

searchDocs.title: Speech Recognition Models​
searchDocs.content: Vosk Models:  Installed Location: /home/root/models/stt/vosk/Small Model: vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15 (~40MB)Large Model: vosk-model-en-us-0.22-lgraph (~128MB)Other Languages: Available at https://alphacephei.com/vosk/modelsModel directory structure: /home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15/ ├── am/ ├── conf/ ├── graph/ ├── ivector/ └── README   Whisper Models:  Installed Location: /home/root/models/stt/whisper/Default Model: ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin (Tiny model, quantized)Available Sizes: tiny, base, small, medium, largeDownload from Whisper.cpp repository or Hugging Face

searchDocs.title: TCP Backend​
searchDocs.content: Runs a JSON server that clients can connect to and receive recognition results in real-time.  # VOSK with TCP backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=S16LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15 tcp-port=9999 # WHISPER with TCP backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=F32LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/whisper/ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin tcp-port=9999 # Connect to receive results nc localhost 9999

searchDocs.title: MQTT Backend​
searchDocs.content: Publishes recognition results to an MQTT topic for distributed processing.  # VOSK with MQTT backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=S16LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15 \ mqtt-broker=localhost \ mqtt-topic=stt/vosk # WHISPER with MQTT backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=F32LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/whisper/ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin \ mqtt-broker=localhost \ mqtt-topic=stt/whisper # Subscribe to results mosquitto_sub -h localhost -t stt/vosk

searchDocs.title: Printf Backend​
searchDocs.content: Outputs recognition results to console/stdout for debugging.  # VOSK with Printf backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=S16LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15 # WHISPER with Printf backend gst-launch-1.0 alsasrc device=hw:1,0 ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! \ audio/x-raw,format=F32LE,channels=1,rate=16000 ! \ dctstt model=/home/root/models/stt/whisper/ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin

searchDocs.title: Output Format​
searchDocs.content: Recognition results are provided in JSON format:  Final Result:  { "text": "hello world" }   Partial Result:  { "partial": "hello wo" }

searchDocs.title: Bus Messages​
searchDocs.content: The plugin posts GStreamer bus messages for integration with applications:  Message Name: stt-final  Structure Fields:  text (string): The recognized textjson (string): Complete JSON result from the speech recognition engine  Example (C):  GstBus *bus = gst_element_get_bus(pipeline); GstMessage *msg = gst_bus_timed_pop_filtered(bus, GST_CLOCK_TIME_NONE, GST_MESSAGE_ELEMENT); if (msg && gst_message_has_name(msg, "stt-final")) { const GstStructure *s = gst_message_get_structure(msg); const gchar *text = gst_structure_get_string(s, "text"); g_print("Recognized: %s\n", text); }

searchDocs.title: Test Applications​
searchDocs.content: The STT plugin provides two test executables that are built as part of the STT plugin build process and installed to /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/. Each test executable corresponds to one speech recognition engine:

searchDocs.title: 1. Vosk STT Test (test_stt_vosk)​
searchDocs.content: Tests the Vosk speech recognition engine with WER (Word Error Rate) calculation.  Location: /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/test_stt_vosk  ./test_stt_vosk <model_path> <audio_file.wav> <reference.txt>   Arguments:  model_path - Path to Vosk model directoryaudio_file.wav - WAV audio file (S16LE, 16kHz, mono)reference.txt - Reference transcription for comparison  Example:  ./test_stt_vosk \ /home/root/models/stt/vosk/vosk-model-small-en-us-0.15 \ /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/sample.wav \ /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/sample.txt   What it does:  Loads the Vosk modelReads the WAV file and validates format (16kHz, mono, 16-bit)Processes audio in 4000-sample chunks (simulating streaming)Shows partial and final recognition results as audio is processedCalls finalize() at end of file to retrieve any remaining buffered textCalculates WER by comparing with reference textReturns exit code 0 if WER < 50%, else 1  Finalize Method The Vosk backend's finalize() method is important for file-based processing. It retrieves any remaining text that Vosk has buffered but not yet returned as a final result. This ensures complete transcription when the audio stream ends.  Audio Format Requirements:  Format: S16LE (16-bit signed PCM)Sample Rate: 16000 HzChannels: 1 (mono)

searchDocs.title: 2. Whisper STT Test (test_stt_whisper)​
searchDocs.content: Tests the Whisper speech recognition engine with WER calculation.  Location: /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/test_stt_whisper  ./test_stt_whisper <model_path> <audio_file.wav> <reference.txt>   Arguments:  model_path - Path to Whisper GGML model fileaudio_file.wav - WAV audio file (16kHz, mono)reference.txt - Reference transcription for comparison  Example:  ./test_stt_whisper \ /home/root/models/stt/whisper/ggml-tiny.en-q5_1.bin \ /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/sample.wav \ /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/sample.txt   What it does:  Loads the Whisper model with default settings (4 threads)Configures batch mode (streaming=false) for file processingReads the WAV file and converts to F32LE formatValidates format (16kHz, mono)Processes audio in 48000-sample chunks (3 seconds at 16kHz)Accumulates all audio data during process_audio() callsCalls finalize() at end of file to perform full transcriptionCalculates WER by comparing with reference textReturns exit code 0 if WER < 50%, else 1  Batch Mode vs Streaming Mode The Whisper backend supports two processing modes via the streaming parameter: Streaming mode (streaming=true, default): Processes audio chunks in real-time as they arrive. Suitable for live audio capture where immediate feedback is needed.Batch mode (streaming=false): Accumulates all audio and processes the complete buffer on finalize(). Provides better quality results with no duplicate segments. The test application uses this mode for file processing. For file-based testing, batch mode is recommended as it processes the entire audio at once, resulting in more accurate transcriptions.  Audio Format Requirements:  Input Format: 16-bit PCM (auto-converted to F32LE)Sample Rate: 16000 HzChannels: 1 (mono)

searchDocs.title: Test Data​
searchDocs.content: The plugin includes test data automatically installed at /usr/bin/tests/sentinel-sdk/stt/ via the BitBake recipe:  File	Descriptionsample.wav	Sample audio file (S16LE, 16kHz, mono) sample.txt	Reference transcription

searchDocs.title: Word Error Rate (WER) Calculation​
searchDocs.content: Both test applications calculate WER to measure recognition accuracy:  WER Formula:  WER = (Substitutions + Deletions + Insertions) / Total Words × 100% Accuracy = 100% - WER   WER Interpretation:  WER < 10%: Excellent recognitionWER 10-20%: Good recognitionWER 20-30%: Acceptable recognitionWER 30-50%: Poor recognition (warning threshold)WER > 50%: Very poor recognition (test fails)

searchDocs.title: High WER (Poor Recognition)​
searchDocs.content: If WER is very high:  Check audio quality: Ensure clear speech with minimal background noiseVerify correct sample rate (16kHz)Check that audio is not clipped or distorted Check reference text: Ensure reference transcription exactly matches the audioUse lowercase, no punctuation (WER normalizes text) Try different model: Vosk: Try larger model (vosk-model-en-us-0.22-lgraph)Whisper: Try larger model (ggml-base.en.bin or ggml-small.en.bin) Check language match: Ensure model language matches audio languageUse language-specific models when available
